units.title: Introductions I: Before You Start and Making Entries
units.summary: Know what this syllabus is, who it is for, the time it needs, when the exam is, and how entries and retakes work.

sections.h: Welcome: what this course will do for you
p: This course helps you to teach Cambridge IGCSE Religious Studies (0490) with confidence. You do not need to be an expert on every religion today. You need to know what the exam asks, how to plan the course, how to teach religion fairly and how to help students earn marks.

In Week 1 you will learn how the syllabus works, how entries, access arrangements and grades work, how Cambridge plans a whole-school curriculum, how Cambridge teachers teach, and what the syllabus overview says. Weeks 2 to 6 follow after this.
Key points:
• Syllabus: Cambridge IGCSE Religious Studies 0490, for exams in 2025, 2026 and 2027.
• Course length: 6 weeks online. Week 1 is open now.
• Language: simple words, short steps, bullet points and pictures.

ex.t: By the end of Week 1 you will be able to
b: Explain the aims, content, papers and assessment objectives of 0490.
Tell your exams officer what they need to do and when.
Describe the Cambridge Pathway and plan time for Religious Studies.
Use the Cambridge learner attributes in your classroom.
Make a first plan for your teaching year.

sections.h: Why choose this syllabus?
p: Cambridge IGCSE is the world's most popular international qualification for 14 to 16 year olds, although other ages can take it. It is tried, tested and trusted.
Key facts:
• Students can choose from about 70 subjects in any combination.
• It is taught in over 4,500 schools in more than 140 countries.
• Programmes balance knowledge and understanding of the subject with skills for the next steps in education or work.

• IGCSE Religious Studies builds transferable skills: a reflective understanding of values, opinions and attitudes, and the ability to present and analyse different viewpoints and the ideas they are based on.

ex.t: What students become (the Cambridge learner attributes)
b: Confident: explores ideas, understands social, religious and moral concepts, and expresses views.
Responsible: sees how complex and sensitive religious debates are, including challenges to belief and practice today.
Reflective: knows there are many viewpoints and thinks about how they are supported.
Innovative: explores different religious understandings of the world, including views different from their own.
Engaged: works with the diversity of belief and practice in its cultural setting.

sections.h: Recognition and what comes next
p: Cambridge IGCSEs are accepted by leading universities and employers as evidence of academic achievement. UK NARIC (now UK ENIC) found Cambridge IGCSE comparable to the UK GCSE.
Key points for students and parents:
• Students with grades A* to C are well prepared for courses such as Cambridge International AS and A Level Divinity and Islamic Studies.
• Many universities ask for a mix of AS and A Levels and IGCSEs, or equivalent.
• You can read more at www.cambridgeinternational.org/recognition.

b: 'This qualification is accepted worldwide, builds reading, thinking and writing skills, and prepares students for AS and A Level.'

sections.h: Before you start: previous study and time
p: Previous study: Cambridge does not expect students to have studied Religious Studies before. You can start from the beginning.

Guided learning hours: Cambridge designs IGCSE syllabuses to need about 130 guided learning hours for each subject. This is guidance only. The real number depends on your school and on what students already know.
Key points:
• Guided learning hours means time when a teacher teaches or guides the students.
• Count your real teaching weeks and lessons (you will plan this in more detail later in the course).
• If students are new to the subject or find English difficult, they may need more time.

b: 2 lessons a week x 60 minutes = 2 hours a week.
32 teaching weeks a year x 2 hours = 64 hours a year.
Two years = 128 hours, close to the 130-hour guide.

sections.h: Availability, zones and timetables
p: Every Cambridge school belongs to one of six administrative zones. Each zone has its own exam timetable. This keeps exams secure.
Key points:
• This syllabus is not available in all zones. Check www.cambridgeinternational.org/0490 to see if it is available to you.
• You can see your zone's timetable at www.cambridgeinternational.org/timetables.
• For this syllabus you can enter candidates in the November exam series.
• Always use the syllabus for the year in which the candidate will sit the exam.
• Private candidates can enter. Read the Cambridge Guide to Making Entries first.

b: Students start in January 2026 and sit in November 2027: use the 2025 to 2027 syllabus.
Always check the front cover: 'syllabus for 2025, 2026 and 2027'.
Sign up for syllabus update emails at www.cambridgeinternational.org/syllabusupdates.

sections.h: Combining with other syllabuses and group awards
p: Students can take this syllabus together with other Cambridge International syllabuses in one exam series. There are only two exceptions.
Key points:
• They cannot take Cambridge O Level Biblical Studies 2035 in the same series.
• They cannot take any syllabus with the same title at the same level. Cambridge IGCSE, IGCSE (9-1) and O Level are all at the same level.

• Cambridge ICE (International Certificate of Education) is a group award for IGCSE. It recognises students who pass in a range of subjects, which supports a broad and balanced curriculum. See www.cambridgeinternational.org/cambridgeice.

b: A student takes IGCSE Religious Studies, English, Mathematics, Biology and History in the same series: allowed.
A student tries to take IGCSE Religious Studies and O Level Biblical Studies together: not allowed.

sections.h: Making entries: who does what
p: Exams officers send entries to Cambridge International. They should work closely with you so that the right number of candidates are entered for the right syllabus components. The entry option codes and instructions are in the Cambridge Guide to Making Entries, which your exams officer has.
Key points:
• To keep exams secure, Cambridge makes question papers for different areas, called administrative zones. An entry option code shows which components a candidate takes for that zone.
• Your exams officer gets support and guidance for the whole exams cycle at www.cambridgeinternational.org/eoguide.
• Retakes: candidates can retake the whole qualification as many times as they want. Information is at www.cambridgeinternational.org/retakes.
• Language: the syllabus and assessment materials are in English only.

ex.t: A short list for your first meeting with the exams officer
b: Which zone are we in, and is 0490 available?
Which series will our students sit?
When is the entry deadline?
Who will check access arrangements?
Where is the Cambridge Handbook?

sections.h: Before you start: your full checklist
p: Syllabus section 5, 'What else you need to know', starts with 'Before you start'. Use this checklist.
• Previous study: no previous study of Religious Studies is expected. Start with the basics and check students' English reading level.
• Guided learning hours: about 130 for the subject. Add up your real lessons. This is guidance only. Needs vary with the school and the learners' experience.
• Availability: this syllabus is not available in all administrative zones. Check www.cambridgeinternational.org/0490.
• Timetable: find your zone's timetable at www.cambridgeinternational.org/timetables. Give the dates to your exams officer.
• Exam series: you can enter candidates in the November series.
• Syllabus year: use the syllabus for the year the candidate takes the exam. This course follows the 2025, 2026 and 2027 syllabus.
• Private candidates: they can enter. Read the Cambridge Guide to Making Entries.
• Combining syllabuses: the only exceptions are Cambridge O Level Biblical Studies 2035 and syllabuses with the same title at the same level.
• Group awards: Cambridge ICE recognises success in a range of subjects.

b: Write down your guided learning hours.
Confirm availability and zone timetable.
Check the syllabus year.
Share the dates with your exams officer.
Note any students who may need access arrangements.

sections.h: Making entries: step-by-step with the exams officer
p: Syllabus section 5 also explains 'Making entries'. Teachers and exams officers work together.
• Who: exams officers submit entries to Cambridge International.
• What they need from you: the number of candidates, whether any are private candidates, whether anyone needs access arrangements, and the right components (Paper 1 and Paper 2 for all candidates).
• Entry option codes and instructions: in the Cambridge Guide to Making Entries. Your exams officer has a copy.

• Exam administration: to keep exams secure, papers are produced for different administrative zones. Each zone has its own timetable. An entry option code identifies the components a candidate takes for that zone.
• Support: Cambridge supports exams officers at www.cambridgeinternational.org/eoguide.
• Retakes: candidates can retake the whole qualification as many times as they want. See www.cambridgeinternational.org/retakes.
• Language: the syllabus and assessment materials are in English only.

ex.t: A simple entry timeline (adapt to your exam series)
b: Start of the course: check availability, zone and access arrangements.
Several months before the exam: confirm candidate numbers and final entries with the exams officer.
Before the exam: confirm the timetable, rooms and invigilation.
After the exam: wait for results and plan any retakes.

units.title: Introductions II: Accessibility, After the Exam and Using the Grades
units.summary: Understand access arrangements, how grades and results are reported, how teachers and students use grades, and what changed in the 2025 to 2027 syllabus.

sections.h: Accessibility and equality: fair for all students
p: Cambridge works to avoid direct or indirect discrimination. It designs syllabuses and exam materials to be as inclusive as possible for candidates of all national, cultural or social backgrounds, and for candidates with protected characteristics.
Key points:
• Protected characteristics include special educational needs and disability, religion and belief, and characteristics related to gender and identity.
• Language and layout of papers are made as accessible as possible.
• This gives every candidate the fairest chance to show what they know, and reduces the need for reasonable adjustments.

ex.t: Why this matters in Religious Studies
b: You will teach students of many beliefs and of no belief. Every student must feel respected.
Never treat a student's own faith as a problem or as proof of knowledge.
Exam questions are about knowledge and evaluation, not about what a student personally believes.

sections.h: Access arrangements
p: Access arrangements (including modified papers) are the main way Cambridge makes 'reasonable adjustments', guided by the UK Equality Act (2010), for candidates with special educational needs (SEN), disability, illness or injury. They help candidates by reducing barriers and giving them a better chance to show their knowledge, skills and understanding.
Important points:
• A request should be based on evidence of the candidate's barrier, and should also match the candidate's normal way of working at school.
• Cambridge must agree that it is a reasonable adjustment, has a reasonable cost and timeframe, and does not affect the security and integrity of the exam.
• Check at the start of the course which arrangements are available. Details are in the Cambridge Handbook at www.cambridgeinternational.org/eoguide.
• If you need something not on the standard list, contact Cambridge at the start of the course.
• Candidates who cannot access parts of the assessment may receive an award based on the parts they completed.

b: Date, student, barrier seen (for example, slow reading speed).
Support used in class and in tests (extra time, large print).
Result and who was told (parents, exams officer).
Keep this evidence from the first term, not the last month.

sections.h: After the exam: grading and reporting
p: Grades A*, A, B, C, D, E, F or G show the standard a candidate reached. A* is the highest and G is the lowest. 'Ungraded' means the candidate's performance did not reach the standard for grade G. Ungraded is shown on the statement of results but not on the certificate.
Key points:
• On a statement of results, you may see Q (pending) or X (no result). These letters do not appear on the certificate.
• On results and certificates, Cambridge IGCSE is shown as International General Certificate of Secondary Education (IGCSE).
• For this syllabus, all candidates take two papers and are eligible for grades A* to G.

ex.t: Example: explaining a result to a parent
b: Grade B: 'Your child shows good knowledge and can evaluate different views.'
Ungraded: 'The work did not reach grade G. We can plan a retake.'
Q: 'The result is pending. We will tell you when Cambridge releases it.'

sections.h: How students and teachers can use the grades
p: Assessment at Cambridge IGCSE has two purposes. First, it measures learning and achievement: it confirms performance against the knowledge, understanding and skills in the syllabus, at the levels in the grade descriptions. Second, it shows likely future success: results help predict who is well prepared for a course or career, and help students choose the best course or career.
Key points for teachers:
• Look at results by paper and by question. Which religion and which topics lost the most marks?
• Compare AO1 (knowledge) marks with AO2 (evaluation) marks. Many students score well on knowledge but lose marks on evaluation.
• Use Cambridge results analysis and principal examiner reports for teachers to plan the next year.
• Share clear next steps with students: what they can do now and what to do to reach the next grade.

b: 5 minutes: headline results.
10 minutes: find the weakest topic and weakest question type.
10 minutes: choose two teaching changes.
5 minutes: write who does what and when to review.

sections.h: Grade descriptions
p: Grade descriptions give an idea of the standard of work candidates at certain grades are likely to show. Weakness in one part of the exam can be balanced by a better performance in another part.
Key point:
• For this syllabus, grade descriptions will be published after the first assessment in 2025. Check the Cambridge website and School Support Hub for the latest version.

b: Use the specimen mark schemes. They include the levels-of-response marking grids for AO1 and AO2.
Practise marking a few answers with the grids before you teach the first lesson.
Look for the grade descriptions when they are published and add them to your teacher file.

sections.h: What changed in the 2025, 2026 and 2027 syllabus
p: The syllabus was reviewed and revised for first exam in 2025. Cambridge says you must read the whole syllabus before planning your teaching programme.
Key changes:
• The subject content is more detailed. The wording is longer, but what you teach is largely the same.
• Some content was added or removed after subject expert advice.
• New topic in all three religions: Stewardship of the environment. Ethical debates on the treatment of animals are not included.
• New topic in Islam: The five roots of Usul ad-Din.
• Christianity content removed: the difference between a bishop and an archbishop; types of Bible literature (history, myth, psalms, songs, prophecy); tithing.
• Islam content removed: Jihad (greater and lesser).
• Judaism content removed: knowledge of the Tenakh, Mishnah and Talmud; the festivals Simchat Torah and Shavuot.
• Content is now divided between Paper 1 and Paper 2.
• In the Judaism section, God is spelled G-d.
• Some section names changed slightly, and learner attributes were added.

b: Old textbooks and past papers may include removed content. Check each topic against the syllabus.
Spelling: candidates are not penalised for using a different version of a spelling, as long as it is clear which word they mean.

sections.h: Accessibility and equality: the full picture for teachers
p: Syllabus section 5 has a heading 'Accessibility and equality' with two parts.

• Syllabus and assessment design: Cambridge works to avoid direct or indirect discrimination. It designs syllabuses and assessment materials to be as inclusive as possible for candidates of all national, cultural or social backgrounds and candidates with protected characteristics (special educational needs and disability, religion and belief, characteristics related to gender and identity). Language and layout are designed to make the materials accessible, so that all candidates have the fairest chance to show their knowledge, skills and understanding. This reduces the need for reasonable adjustments.

• Access arrangements: including modified papers. They are the main way Cambridge meets its duty, as guided by the UK Equality Act (2010), to make reasonable adjustments for candidates with SEN, disability, illness or injury. They help when a candidate would otherwise be at a substantial disadvantage.
How this helps you teach Religious Studies:
• Notice early which students need support with reading, writing, hearing or sight.
• Use clear, short sentences and glossaries of religious terms.
• Never ask students to reveal their own faith to take part.

ex.t: Examples of barriers and arrangements (to discuss with your exams officer)
b: A student with dyslexia may need extra time or a modified paper.
A student with a hearing difficulty may need adjustments to oral instructions.
A student with an injury to their writing hand may need support to write.
Check the Cambridge Handbook for what is allowed.

sections.h: After the exam: reading results and certificates
p: Syllabus section 5 explains 'After the exam'.
• Grades A*, A, B, C, D, E, F or G show the standard achieved. A* is the highest, G is the lowest.
• Ungraded: the performance did not meet the standard required for grade G. It is reported on the statement of results but not on the certificate.
• Q (pending) and X (no result): may appear on statements of results, not on the certificate.
• On results and certificates the qualification is shown as International General Certificate of Secondary Education (IGCSE).
• For 0490, candidates sit two papers (80 marks each) and receive one overall grade from A* to G.
After results, what should teachers do?
• Check every student's result against expectations.
• Ask your exams officer about retakes, and about Cambridge results services.
• Use results to plan teaching for the next year.

b: Start with what they did well.
Explain the grade in plain words.
Show the next step: retake, AS or A Level, or another course.
Keep the tone kind and honest.

sections.h: How students and teachers can use the grades: worked examples
p: The syllabus names two purposes of assessment: to measure learning and achievement, and to show likely future success.
Use for students:
• A student with grade B or above in 0490 may be well prepared for AS Level Divinity or Islamic Studies and for subjects that need essay writing and evaluation.
• A student with grade D may need to strengthen evaluation skills before AS Level, or may choose another route.
• Grades help students choose courses and careers.
Use for teachers:
• Compare your class results with last year's results.
• Look for the questions and topics where marks were lost, using results analysis and principal examiner reports.
• Compare AO1 and AO2: if students did well on knowledge but poorly on evaluation, teach more part (c) practice.
• Set targets and write actions: for example, 'Add one evaluation task to every unit'.
• Share results with colleagues to improve the whole department.

b: Class average: AO1 strong, AO2 weak.
Action: weekly 15-minute evaluation practice with the PEEL-J pattern.
Check progress after four weeks with a short test.
Share improvements at the next staff meeting.

sections.h: Grade descriptions: how to prepare while they are unpublished
p: The syllabus has a heading 'Grade descriptions'. Grade descriptions give an idea of the standards of achievement that candidates awarded certain grades are likely to show. A weakness in one part of the exam can be balanced by better performance in another.
The syllabus says grade descriptions for Religious Studies will be published after the first assessment in 2025. What to do now:
• Check the Cambridge website and the School Support Hub for updates and sign up for syllabus update emails.
• Use the specimen mark schemes and levels-of-response grids to understand standards.
• Use examiner reports as they become available.
• Keep a folder of sample answers at different levels, with notes on why they earned those marks.

ex.t: Build your own working scale (a classroom tool, not an official grade description)
b: Strong: accurate detail, clear explanation, several views with evidence, reasoned judgement.
Secure: mostly accurate, some explanation, two views, simple judgement.
Developing: some facts, little explanation, one view, no clear judgement.
Replace with official descriptions when published.

sections.h: Changes to this syllabus for 2025, 2026 and 2027: what to do about each
p: The syllabus was reviewed and revised for first examination in 2025. Cambridge says you must read the whole syllabus before planning your teaching.
Make a list of what to do with each change.
• More detailed subject content: use the lettered points in Section 3 as your checklist, but do not teach more than the syllabus asks.
• Some content added or removed: compare any old notes with the new Section 3.
• New topic, Stewardship of the environment (all three religions): add a lesson in the Religion and social action block. Animal ethics is not included.
• New topic, five roots of Usul ad-Din (Islam): add a lesson on Shi'ah beliefs.
• Removed Christianity content: difference between a bishop and an archbishop; types of Bible literature (history, myth, psalms, songs, prophecy); tithing.
• Removed Islam content: Jihad (greater and lesser).
• Removed Judaism content: knowledge of the Tenakh, Mishnah and Talmud; the festivals Simchat Torah and Shavuot.
• Content divided between Paper 1 and Paper 2.
• In Judaism, G-d is spelt G-d.
• Some section names changed slightly.
• Learner attributes were added to the syllabus.

b: Take your old scheme of work and cross out removed topics.
Highlight new topics in a different colour.
Check textbooks and websites for removed content.
Note any new resources you need.

units.title: Implementing the Curriculum I: What a Curriculum Is and 12 Principles
units.summary: Learn what 'curriculum' means in Cambridge schools and the twelve principles for planning and running a good one.

sections.h: Introduction: why teachers need this
p: This part uses the Cambridge guide 'Implementing the Curriculum with Cambridge'. It is written for school leaders, but teachers need it too, because teachers turn the plan into real lessons.
Key points:
• Cambridge gives schools a rich menu of options, not one fixed recipe.
• School leaders and teachers do the most important work: designing the curriculum for their own students, culture and values.
• When you finish this part you can explain what a curriculum is, describe the Cambridge Pathway, plan time for your subject and teach in the way Cambridge hopes its teachers will.

b: 1. Curriculum planning: an overview (this unit).
2. Designing the school curriculum (next two units).
3. Approaches to teaching and learning (the unit after).
4. Then the syllabus overview for 0490.

sections.h: 1.1 What is curriculum?
p: People use the word 'curriculum' in different ways around the world. Some use it widely (subjects, links between them, teaching methods and school life). Others use it narrowly (only a list of courses or one programme). Cambridge uses four clear definitions.
The four meanings:
• School curriculum: the whole combination of subjects a learner studies in a school year and in later years.
• Subject curriculum: the content and skills in one syllabus, spread across stages of learning.
• Co-curricular curriculum: valued activities outside lessons that the school supports, such as clubs, sport and music.
• Experienced curriculum: what learners actually receive, including the planned and unplanned results of school life.

ex.t: Example: four curricula in one school
b: School curriculum: Religious Studies, English, Mathematics, Science and others.
Subject curriculum: the IGCSE Religious Studies 0490 syllabus.
Co-curricular: interfaith club, debating society, school assembly.
Experienced: what students really learn, including from how adults treat people of different beliefs.

sections.h: 1.1 continued: the wider learning experience
p: A good school gives more than the total of its subjects. Learning does not begin or end in the classroom. What learners really experience can differ from what is written, because many things act together.
What shapes the experienced curriculum:
• The school's vision and values.
• The quality of teaching.
• What learners already know and how motivated they are.
• School leadership and culture.
• The subject curricula and assessment habits.
• The school's internal structures.
Every school should check regularly whether the experience matches its intentions.

ex.t: A one-minute check for your class
b: Ask: 'What is one thing you learned this week that was not on my plan?'
Collect answers on paper without names.
Read them. They show the experienced curriculum in your classroom.

sections.h: Vision, mission and planning questions
p: A school vision is a clear picture of where the school wants to go, shared by the whole community. A mission statement says the school's purpose. The school strategic plan turns the vision into actions, usually with priorities for up to five years and a detailed plan for the next year.
Questions a school should answer when planning its curriculum:
• Learners: What academic, personal and social outcomes do we want? Which skills? How will it motivate and challenge them?
• Teachers: Which teaching and assessment practices are central? What professional development is needed?

• Structure: Which Cambridge programmes will we use? How will we support learners who do not have English as a first language? How many hours for each subject? Will learners have choice? What facilities and money are needed?

ex.t: Questions a Religious Studies department can ask
b: Which two religions will we teach, and why?
Which teachers have knowledge of each religion, and who needs support?
How will we make sure every student feels respected?
How many hours do we have, and how will we use them?
How will we check that students really understand?

sections.h: 1.2 Principles 1 to 4
p: Cambridge believes twelve principles matter in every school.
Principle 1: The school curriculum should be broad, balanced and consistent, with clear and smooth progression for all learners.
• Quality is more important than quantity: too much content leaves no time for deep understanding.
• Use a spiral approach: each stage returns to key ideas and builds on them.
• Balance usually includes mathematics, languages, sciences, technology, humanities, creative arts and physical education.
• Schools write their own schemes of work, because the curriculum is built locally.
Principle 2: The instructional system should be well aligned and coherent. Curriculum, pedagogy (how we teach) and assessment must fit together.
Principle 3: The curriculum should develop learners and teachers who are confident, responsible, reflective, innovative and engaged.
Principle 4: Each subject curriculum should give inspiring, relevant content with the right breadth and depth, arranged in a learning spiral.

b: Early: describe the main features of a church, mosque or synagogue.
Later: explain what they mean to believers.
Final stage: evaluate different views on how important they are.
Same topic, rising demand.

sections.h: 1.2 Principles 5 to 8
p: Principle 5: The curriculum should recognise each learner's language background and give the support they need. All Cambridge qualifications are assessed in English.
• Keep developing each learner's first language too: it supports thinking, identity and international understanding.
• Make all teachers language aware: plan language support in every subject lesson.
• Cambridge supports bilingual education and CLIL (content and language integrated learning).
• Examiners mark positively. Learners are not penalised for spelling and grammar except in tests of language skills.
Principle 6: Assessment has several purposes: feedback during learning (assessment for learning) and judging the standard reached (summative).
Principle 7: Clear and meaningful standards are needed to measure progress and compare fairly across the world.
Principle 8: Teachers are the most powerful influence on learning. They should also show the learner attributes and keep learning through reflective practice and professional development.

ex.t: Being language aware in Religious Studies
b: Teach key words with meaning and example: pilgrimage, sacrament, creed, fasting.
Give sentence starters: 'This matters to Muslims because ...'.
Let students discuss in pairs before writing.
Give feedback on ideas first and language second.

sections.h: 1.2 Principles 9 to 12
p: Principle 9: To get the best results, learners must be actively engaged.
• Understanding is built in the learner's own mind. It cannot be passed from teacher to learner like a parcel.
• Teachers listen to the learner's voice, challenge it and lead learning actively, then change their teaching using feedback.
Principle 10: Strong leadership is needed for lasting improvement. Teachers can lead too.
Principle 11: Curriculum development is ongoing. Schools gather evidence, ask 'Is it delivering what we want? How do we know? What do students think?' and then improve.
Principle 12: The curriculum must help all learners reach their potential, whatever their starting point.

ex.t: Self-check: which principle do you need most this term?
b: Principle 9 if your lessons are mostly teacher talk.
Principle 5 if students struggle with English.
Principle 11 if you have never collected feedback from students.
Write one action for your chosen principle.

units.title: Implementing the Curriculum II: The Cambridge Pathway and Its Stages
units.summary: See the four stages of the Cambridge Pathway with pictures, and learn what each stage offers, including where IGCSE Religious Studies fits.

sections.h: 2.1 The Cambridge Pathway
p: The Cambridge Pathway gives students a clear path for educational success from age 5 to 19. It has four stages, shown in the picture below. Age ranges are only for guidance. Cambridge Professional Development supports teachers and school leaders at every stage.
Key points:
• Cambridge Primary: ages 5 to 11.
• Cambridge Lower Secondary: ages 11 to 14.
• Cambridge Upper Secondary: ages 14 to 16 (IGCSE, O Level, ICE Certificate).
• Cambridge Advanced: ages 16 to 19 (AS and A Level, Pre-U, AICE Diploma, IPQ).
• Schools do not have to use the whole Pathway. They can choose some stages or combine Cambridge with national programmes.

b: There is a difference between the written Cambridge programme and the curriculum taught in your school. Teachers can add local content and case studies.
IGCSE (or O Level) at the end of Upper Secondary gives an international standard and opens the way to AS and A Level.

img.alt: The Cambridge Pathway: Primary 5 to 11, Lower Secondary 11 to 14, Upper Secondary 14 to 16, Advanced 16 to 19, with Cambridge Professional Development underneath
img.cap: The Cambridge Pathway: a clear path for educational success from age 5 to 19. Source: Cambridge International, Implementing the Curriculum with Cambridge.

sections.h: 2.2 Cambridge Primary
p: Cambridge Primary is for learners aged 5 to 11. It has curriculum frameworks in 10 subjects, including English, English as a second language, Mathematics, Science and Cambridge Global Perspectives.
Key points:
• Each framework has six stages, usually one stage a year, but schools can use shorter or longer periods.
• No subject is compulsory. Schools choose what fits.
• Progression Tests (stage 3 to 6) can be used when the teacher thinks the class is ready and are marked by the teacher.
• The Primary Checkpoint at the end of the programme is marked by Cambridge, with feedback on strengths and weaknesses.

b: If your students come from a Cambridge Primary school, ask for Checkpoint reports.
Religious or moral education at this age may be taught through the school's own curriculum.
Build on what they know instead of starting from nothing.

sections.h: 2.3 Cambridge Lower Secondary
p: Cambridge Lower Secondary is for learners aged 11 to 14. It builds on Primary and prepares students for Upper Secondary.
Key points:
• It is a three-stage programme with frameworks in the same subjects as Primary.
• No part is compulsory.
• Cambridge reviews each framework so learners are ready for the next stage.
• Progression Tests for each stage and the Lower Secondary Checkpoint at the end (marked by Cambridge) give feedback on achievement.

b: Many students will have met world religions in school lessons before IGCSE.
Ask them what they already know and what they are curious about.
Use the Cambridge Global Perspectives skills (evidence, argument, perspectives) as a bridge to evaluation in IGCSE.

sections.h: 2.4 Cambridge Upper Secondary (where 0490 sits)
p: Cambridge Upper Secondary is for ages 14 to 16. It offers more than 70 IGCSE subjects and more than 40 O Level subjects. IGCSE Religious Studies 0490 is in this stage.
Key points:
• IGCSE means International General Certificate of Secondary Education. Each subject is certificated separately.
• Grades are A* to G. The UK treats Cambridge IGCSE as equivalent to the GCSE.
• O Level is similar but graded A* to E.
• Students usually study IGCSE over one or two years in school. About 130 hours are planned for each subject.
• Some subjects have barred combinations: students cannot take both in the same exam series. For 0490, the exception is O Level Biblical Studies 2035.
• Some subjects have core and extended tiers. Religious Studies 0490 does not: all candidates take the same two papers.

b: Over 70 IGCSE subjects.
About 130 guided learning hours per subject.
0490: no tiers, two written papers, grades A* to G.
Check the barred combinations in the syllabus and Handbook before making entries.

sections.h: 2.5 Cambridge Advanced
p: Cambridge Advanced is for ages 16 to 19. Learners often want to specialise by now. It includes Cambridge International AS and A Level (more than 50 subjects), Cambridge Pre-U (in the UK), the AICE Diploma and Global Perspectives and Research.
Key points:
• An AS Level has half the content of an A Level. It can be taken alone after one year or as the first half of an A Level.
• A Level grades are A* to E, in standard with UK A Levels. There is no A* in AS Level.
• Cambridge Divinity and Islamic Studies at AS and A Level are natural next steps for students with strong IGCSE Religious Studies grades.
• There are three planning approaches: non-staged (all A Level papers at the end of year 2), staged (AS in year 1 and/or 2, then A Level) and AS only. Check what universities want before you decide.
• Teaching time: about 180 hours for AS and 360 hours for A Level (including directed study).

ex.t: Why Religious Studies teachers should know this
b: Many of your students will choose AS and A Level subjects after IGCSE. Their grades help them choose.
Some universities ask for specific subjects and grades. Ask your school counsellor.
Help students see how IGCSE skills (evidence, argument, evaluation) are used at AS and A Level.

units.title: Implementing the Curriculum III: English, Timetabling, Different School Years and Bilingual Schools
units.summary: Plan language support, time and structure: Cambridge English options, recommended hours, timetables, stage structures and bilingual models.

sections.h: 2.6 English language development and showing English proficiency
p: Religious Studies exams are in English, so English matters for your students. Cambridge International offers English as a school subject, with pathways for first-language learners, bilingual learners and second-language learners. Its sister organisation, Cambridge Assessment English, offers English language qualifications that universities, governments and employers accept.
Key points:
• Both reference the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR): a six-point scale from A1 (beginner) to C2 (mastery).
• Cambridge International English as a Second Language is for schools where part or all of the curriculum is taught in English. It runs through the Pathway from Primary to Upper Secondary.
• Cambridge English programmes for schools suit contexts where English is the only subject taught in English and close CEFR alignment is a priority.

• Universities in English-speaking countries set their own language rules. Some accept a good grade in IGCSE English as a Second Language, others require First Language English. In the UK some courses need a Secure English Language Test such as IELTS.

b: A1 and A2: basic user (simple everyday sentences).
B1 and B2: independent user (can deal with most situations and give reasons).
C1 and C2: proficient user (fluent and precise).
Students need enough English to read the question papers and write clear, reasoned answers.

img.alt: Figure 2: Cambridge English assessments mapped to the CEFR scale from Pre A1 to C2
img.cap: Figure 2: Cambridge Assessment English language assessments for schools, shown against the CEFR scale. Source: Cambridge International, Implementing the Curriculum with Cambridge.

sections.h: 2.7 Timetabling the curriculum: what affects it
p: After designing the curriculum, schools must make a timetable. The timetable depends on the school context, local laws and practice, and the school's budget.
What shapes decisions inside the school:
• The length of the school day, days a week and school year.
• How much choice learners have, and co-curricular activities.
• Extra courses with no exam (for example religious education, values, student leadership).
• Whether classes are mixed-year (multi-levelling) or set by ability.
What limits the timetable:
• Number of teachers and support staff, their contracts and experience.
• Classrooms and special rooms, and resources for language support and special needs.

b: How long is each lesson?
Do we have double periods?
Who teaches Religious Studies, and are they also teaching other subjects?
Can students choose Religious Studies, or is it compulsory?

sections.h: 2.7 continued: recommended guided learning hours
p: Cambridge suggests teaching hours for each stage. The table below shows them.
Key numbers for Religious Studies teachers:
• Upper Secondary (IGCSE and O Level): about 130 hours per subject before the assessments.
• Advanced: about 180 hours for an AS Level and a further 180 for an A Level (non-staged: 360 hours over two years).
• The hours include teaching time and directed study but not independent study. Students should also have chances for independent study outside timetabled lessons.

b: These hours are for guidance only.
Count your real teaching weeks and see if you meet about 130 hours.

sections.h: 2.7 continued: lesson length and one example timetable
p: The length of a lesson changes how you teach. Short periods tend to become dominated by whole-class teaching. Long lessons are wasted if the teacher has not planned enough varied activity.
Key points:
• In the example below, each day has nine 40-minute periods. Older learners have double periods (80 minutes), so each subject gets four hours and 40 minutes a week.
• Teachers should plan several activities that together meet the aims of the syllabus.
• The school's quality assurance should make sure teachers have the right amount of time for effective lessons.

ex.t: Plan a Religious Studies double period (80 minutes)
b: 10 min: starter and recap.
20 min: teach and model one idea (for example features of a mosque).
25 min: pair or group task (for example, match features to their meaning).
15 min: write a short answer in exam style and self-mark.
10 min: reflection and homework.

sections.h: 2.8 Schools with different numbers of school years
p: The Cambridge Pathway has 13 stages and usually one stage is covered each year. Some countries have 12 years of school, or start later, or compress stages. Cambridge programmes are flexible.
Key points:
• Most schools teach IGCSE over two years (grades 10 and 11, when students are about 16). A few use 18 months or even one year.
• Typically students then take AS Levels in grade 11 or 12 and A Levels in grade 12 or 13.
• Some schools accelerate: Lower Secondary starts a year early, for example in grade 7.
• Some schools compress stages. In one example, stage 7 and half of stage 8 are taught in grade 7, and the rest of stage 8 with stage 9 in grade 8.
• Some schools use option blocks or very flexible pathways, so very able students can take IGCSE courses in one year.

ex.t: What this means for a Religious Studies teacher
b: If your school compresses stages, plan carefully so that no important topic is missed.
Check your students' age and stage before you start.
If time is short, give priority to the topics and skills the exam assesses.

sections.h: 2.9 Curriculum models for bilingual and multilingual schools
p: Many schools use Cambridge for the English-medium part of a bilingual programme and use the national curriculum for the first-language part. The best model depends on the school's vision, staff, resources and how much English learners hear outside school.
Key points:
• Models differ in how long they last (short or long term) and how strong they are (low or high intensity).

• Approach A, split curriculum: some subjects follow the national curriculum in the first language and others follow the international curriculum in English. This avoids a double timetable and works only if both qualifications are officially recognised.
• Approach B, shared subject curriculum: some subjects are taught in both languages, either as an integrated curriculum or as two separate curricula.
• CLIL (content and language integrated learning) is the method Cambridge recommends: teachers support students in learning the language they need for the subject.
• Schools need a training plan so local teachers can build their English and teach in English.

ex.t: Why it matters for Religious Studies
b: A bilingual school may teach Religious Studies in English and national religious education in the first language.
Check where content overlaps so students do not repeat everything.
Teach religious vocabulary in English clearly, with meaning and example.

sections.h: Curriculum mapping to avoid repeating teaching
p: Curriculum mapping means comparing two curricula for a subject and finding the topics and skills they share and where they differ.
Steps:
• List the topics in the national curriculum.
• List the topics in the Cambridge syllabus.
• Mark the overlap and the differences.
• Teach the overlap once and teach the differences separately.

An integrated curriculum means students go to one timetabled class, which saves time, but it needs careful planning and teachers who work together. Separate curricula are easier to run, but some learning may be repeated.

b: National religious education covers: pillars of Islam, festivals, prayer.
0490 Islam covers: mosque features, artefacts, the Qur'an, pilgrimage (Hajj), festivals and fasts, family life and social action.
Overlap: pillars, festivals and prayer. Differences: exam skills and evaluation, which you teach separately.

units.title: Implementing the Curriculum IV: Approaches to Teaching and Learning
units.summary: Learn how a Cambridge teacher teaches: active learning, learner and teacher attributes, reflection, links across subjects, key concepts, collaboration and ICT.

sections.h: 3.1 The Cambridge teacher
p: Excellent teaching, including building the learner attributes, is the biggest influence a school has on learners' results and personal growth. There is no single recipe, and different cultures have strong traditions that should be respected. But research shows some practices help learners.
Key points:
• Understanding cannot be passed from one person to another. It is built in the learner's own mind.
• Teachers must listen to the learner's voice, in class and in written work, and use it to challenge and extend what learners think.
• The best teaching challenges learners beyond what they can do alone. Vygotsky called this the zone of proximal development. Teachers scaffold (support) learning there.
• Cambridge calls this active learning: learners are active, and teachers lead learning actively, not just give information.
• Use a mix of individual tasks, group work and whole-class teaching that includes discussion.
• Use assessment often to check whether learners are reaching the aims, and to help learners see how to improve.

ex.t: Example: scaffolding an answer about a place of worship
b: Show a model answer and ask students what makes it good.
Give a frame: Point, Evidence, Meaning.
Let pairs write the first paragraph together.
Remove support: students write the second paragraph alone.
Give feedback and repeat with less support.

sections.h: 3.1 continued: teachers as role models
p: Outstanding teachers show the Cambridge learner attributes themselves. They are confident, responsible, reflective, innovative and engaged because they:
• Have mastery of their subject and relate ideas so that students appreciate what the subject is about.
• Teach for understanding as well as coverage, returning to key ideas in new contexts (a spiral).
• Connect learning to the real world and to other subjects.
• Scaffold learning in the zone of proximal development.
• Have a learning orientation, not only a performance orientation: they care that students learn well, not just look good.
• Model problem solving and care about the whole development of each learner, including attitudes, emotions and confidence.
• Understand and use assessment for different purposes.
• Use a variety of teaching strategies.
• Are reflective and creative, with ongoing professional learning.
• Work with colleagues and the school community. Cambridge also publishes Cambridge Teacher Standards.

b: I know my subject and can explain it simply.
I teach for understanding, not just to finish the book.
I connect lessons to students' real lives.
I use assessment to help students, not only to give marks.
I learn from colleagues and share ideas.

sections.h: 3.2 The Cambridge learner and teacher attributes
p: Schools want learners who understand their own culture and nation and who also have the skills to be global learners. Cambridge's five attributes aim to build five powerful learning habits. They are shown in the table below.
Key points:
• Confident: works well with information and ideas in a structured, critical way; defends views and respects others. Teachers are confident in their subject and show a love of learning.
• Responsible: takes ownership of learning, sets targets, acts with integrity. Teachers are highly professional and care about the whole development of each student.
• Reflective: understands themselves as learners and builds life-long learning strategies. Teachers reflect on practice through research, evaluation and adaptation.
• Innovative: welcomes new challenges and solves unfamiliar problems. Teachers are creative and flexible.
• Engaged: ready to make a difference. Teachers share knowledge and skills with the wider community.
The attributes are not complete; schools can add their own. They need support in lessons and in co-curricular life, from all school staff.

ex.t: Example: one habit for each attribute in Religious Studies
b: Confident: every student speaks for one minute giving a reasoned view.
Responsible: students keep a respectful-language rule for discussion.
Reflective: students write one sentence on how their view changed and why.
Innovative: students compare how two religions answer the same question.
Engaged: students interview a community member (with permission) about practice.

img.alt: Table 8: Learner and teacher attributes: confident, responsible, reflective, innovative and engaged
img.cap: Table 8: Learner and teacher attributes. Source: Cambridge International, Implementing the Curriculum with Cambridge.

sections.h: 3.2 continued: the Cambridge learner
p: The picture below shows the Cambridge learner: confident, responsible, reflective, innovative and engaged. These attributes are interconnected, and the syllabus uses them to describe what the Religious Studies approach encourages.
In 0490 specifically, Cambridge says learners should be:
• Confident: exploring ideas and expressing views.
• Responsible: recognising the sensitivity of religious debates.
• Reflective: recognising many viewpoints and how they are supported.
• Innovative: exploring understandings different from their own.
• Engaged: with the diversity of belief and practice in its cultural setting.

b: Put the learner circle on the wall.
At the end of a lesson ask: 'Which attribute did we use today?'
Notice and praise the attributes when students show them.

img.alt: The Cambridge learner: confident, responsible, reflective, innovative and engaged
img.cap: The Cambridge learner. Source: Cambridge IGCSE Religious Studies 0490 syllabus for 2025, 2026 and 2027.

sections.h: 3.3 Becoming a reflective learner
p: Reflection means thinking about your own learning and judging your progress accurately. Becoming reflective also needs the other four attributes.
Reflective learners:
• Plan and manage their work and judge their progress accurately.
• Understand themselves as learners.
• Think critically and creatively to overcome barriers.
• Learn from mistakes and see failure as a chance to learn.
• Stay emotionally strong when things go wrong.
• Are confident, but not arrogant, and know that learning is social.

Many schools assume learners will become reflective alone. It is not enough. All teachers should help students learn how to learn, in real lessons. Separate 'study skills' classes tend not to work well. A passive learner who re-reads notes believes understanding can be poured into memory. An active learner asks questions, finds the barrier, tries a plan and checks if it works.

b: What did I do well?
What was hard, and why?
What will I do differently next time?
Keep answers in a learning log and review every month.

sections.h: 3.4 Disciplinary and interdisciplinary approaches
p: Schools design the curriculum around a balance of subjects (disciplines), because each subject teaches ways of thinking that are hard to get from everyday life. Michael Young calls this 'powerful knowledge'. But subjects overlap, and learners should also see links.
Key points:
• Understanding each subject well is the foundation for good interdisciplinary work. Without it, learning becomes shallow.
• Excellent schools expect teachers to plan together so that students can move between subjects.

• Cambridge Global Perspectives is an interdisciplinary programme from Primary to A Level. It teaches students to evaluate evidence and arguments, understand other perspectives and do research and teamwork.
• Information literacy is at the heart of Global Perspectives.

ex.t: Links from Religious Studies to other subjects
b: History: how religious communities and places developed.
Geography: pilgrimage routes and sacred places.
Art and Music: symbols, architecture and worship.
English: writing structured arguments and evaluating different views.
Ask colleagues what texts and skills students use in their subject.

sections.h: 3.5 Using conceptual frameworks to support learning
p: Concepts are ways of grouping ideas to make sense of a complicated world. They give a shared language for understanding and action.
Key points:
• Substantive concepts are part of the content (in geography: river, trade, city).
• Second-order concepts shape the key questions of a subject (in history: cause and consequence, change and continuity).
• A threshold concept is one that, once understood, changes how learners understand a field and helps them move forward.
• Cambridge syllabuses help by naming important concepts, but teachers adapt them to their lessons.
• Key concepts link topics, help learners review and apply knowledge, and help them think like experts.

ex.t: Example: key concepts in Religious Studies (a teaching suggestion, not an official list)
b: Belief and practice: how what people believe shows in what they do.
Community and authority: who leads and how communities decide.
Sacred: what is holy and why.
Tradition and change: what stays the same and what changes.
Evaluation: weighing different points of view and reaching a reasoned judgement.

sections.h: 3.6 Collaboration
p: Students need to function well as team members and leaders, because this matters in life and work. They also need to solve problems collaboratively.
Key points:
• The OECD describes collaborative problem solving as two or more people trying to solve a problem by sharing understanding and effort and pooling knowledge and skills.
• Teams need a shared goal, shared responsibility and roles that can change.
• Students must define the problem, check they share the same understanding, think critically and reflect on how well the group is doing.
• Collaboration is not the same as cooperation. Teachers should know the difference when planning group work.
• Schools can build collaboration through fieldwork, project work, Cambridge Global Perspectives and co-curricular activities.

ex.t: A collaborative task for Religious Studies
b: Groups of four plan a 'Guide to a place of worship' for visitors.
Roles: researcher, writer, designer, presenter.
They agree the goal, divide the work, check each other's facts and present.
At the end they reflect: What worked? What would we change?

sections.h: 3.7 Information literacy and using ICT
p: Using ICT well is an essential skill. Computers, tablets and smartphones are used in classrooms all over the world. The key rule is that technology must support carefully planned teaching and learning goals and not replace them.
Key points:
• Information literacy means finding information and also judging its meaning and reliability.
• Information literacy should be part of every subject.
• An interactive whiteboard that involves the whole class is good use. Using it only to lecture is not.
• Cambridge offers professional development qualifications on using ICT in classrooms.

ex.t: Safe, respectful use of ICT in Religious Studies (suggestions; follow school and exam rules)
b: Teach students to check who wrote a source, when, and what evidence it gives.
Use trusted sources from religious communities and from academic institutions.
Never ask students to say or post their personal beliefs publicly.
Use images and videos of sacred places and festivals respectfully and with the right permission.

Which is NOT one of the five Cambridge learner attributes?

o: To support carefully planned teaching and learning goals, not replace them

units.title: Syllabus Overview: Aims, Content, Papers and Assessment Objectives
units.summary: See the whole shape of 0490: the aims, the six content areas for each religion, the two papers, how marks are given and the two assessment objectives.

sections.h: Aims: what the course is for
p: The aims describe the purpose of any course based on this syllabus. The aims are to enable students to:
• Develop knowledge and understanding of religion, studied in a social context.
• Develop an enquiring and sensitive approach to the study of religion and its contribution to individuals, communities and societies.
• Identify and explore the religious, moral and cultural questions raised in the material they study.
• Explore the ways in which belief is reflected in practice and application in the lives of religious people.
• Develop their interest and enthusiasm for the study of religion.
Cambridge is politically neutral. The syllabus, papers and associated materials do not endorse any political view.

b: Knowledge in context: study a festival and how a community keeps it today.
Sensitive approach: always use respectful words for beliefs and believers.
Questions: ask 'what moral question does this raise?'
Belief and practice: link a teaching to what believers do.
Enthusiasm: invite community speakers or visit places of worship (with permission).

sections.h: Content overview: two religions, six sections
p: Candidates study two religions from three: Christianity, Islam and Judaism. For each religion the content is divided into six sections and two papers. Candidates study the same two religions for both Paper 1 and Paper 2.
Key points:
• The content for each religion is different because traditions, beliefs and practices differ.
• You choose resources and examples. They must suit the learners' age, culture and learning context and follow school policies and local law.
• The syllabus gives you the freedom to design a course that interests and challenges your students.

b: Christianity and Islam (common in many African and Middle Eastern schools).
Islam and Judaism.
Christianity and Judaism.
Choose according to teacher knowledge, community, resources and student needs.

sections.h: Paper 1 content: Worship, Beliefs, Scriptures and Sacred Places
p: Paper 1 covers sections 1, 2 and 3 of each religion.
1. Worship:
• The church, mosque or synagogue as a centre for worship and as the centre of the religious community.
• Key features of the building and their meaning and importance.
• Artefacts used in worship, their use, meaning and importance.
• Public (communal) and private (individual) worship.
• The roles and importance of leaders.
2. Beliefs and scriptures: key teachings from the Bible, Qur'an or Torah, as listed in the subject content.
3. Sacred places, places of pilgrimage and religious importance:
• Why pilgrimage matters.
• Places of pilgrimage and places of religious importance.

ex.t: Example for a lesson: Worship in the mosque
b: Teach: the mihrab, minbar, wudu area and prayer hall, and what each means.
Link: to public worship (Jummah) and private prayer.
Question for students: 'Why is the mosque important to the Muslim community?'

sections.h: Paper 2 content: Festivals, Family Life and Social Action
p: Paper 2 covers sections 4, 5 and 6 of each religion.
4. Festivals and fasts:
• Key festivals and fasts from Christianity, Islam or Judaism, as listed.
• Their meaning and importance and how they are celebrated or practised today.
5. Rites of passage and religion and the family:
• Key rites of passage, including birth rites, marriage ceremonies and funerals.
• Beliefs about family life in different religious communities.
• Tradition and change: traditional family roles for men and women, old and young, and reasons to keep or change them.
6. Religion and social action:
• Religious laws and moral and ethical codes.
• Teachings about love and concern for others.
• Stewardship of the environment (new topic).
• Religious organisations that relieve poverty.

ex.t: Example for a lesson: Stewardship of the environment
b: Teach: a key teaching in each chosen religion on caring for creation.
Link: to a practical action, such as a community tree-planting project.
Evaluate: 'Is caring for the environment the most important duty of believers today?' Remember: ethical debates on animals are not in the syllabus.

sections.h: Assessment overview: two papers
p: All candidates take two written papers and are eligible for grades A* to G.
Paper 1: Worship, Beliefs, Scriptures and Sacred Places.
• 1 hour 45 minutes. 80 marks. 50% of the grade.
• Three sections: A Christianity, B Islam, C Judaism. Candidates answer questions in two of the sections.
• Each section has three structured questions worth 20 marks each. Candidates answer two questions in each of their two chosen sections.
Paper 2: Festivals, Fasts, Family Life and Social Action.
• Same time, marks, weighting and structure as Paper 1.
• Both papers are externally assessed (marked by Cambridge).
• Candidates must answer on the same two religions in both papers.

b: Each paper: 4 questions in total (2 in each chosen section).
4 questions x 20 marks = 80 marks.
Each question: (a) 6 marks, (b) 6 marks, (c) 8 marks.

sections.h: Structure of each question: parts (a), (b) and (c)
p: Every question is worth 20 marks and has three parts. Candidates answer all parts of the chosen questions.

• Part (a): 6 marks, short answer, assesses AO1 Knowledge and understanding. It has two sub-parts (i) and (ii). It usually needs facts. One mark for each relevant point. Teach students to look at how many marks are available.
• Part (b): 6 marks, assesses AO1. It usually needs a fuller description or explanation. Marked with the levels-of-response marking grid for AO1.

• Part (c): 8 marks, assesses AO2 Evaluation, linked to the same topic. It needs a longer structured answer that evaluates different points of view and gives a judgement. Marked with the levels-of-response grid for AO2.

ex.t: Example (not an official question): a question about pilgrimage
b: (a)(i) Identify one place of pilgrimage. (a)(ii) Give one reason pilgrims go there. (1 mark each point, 6 marks in all.)
(b) Explain why pilgrimage is important for believers. (6 marks)
(c) 'Going on pilgrimage is the best way to show faith.' Evaluate this statement. (8 marks)

sections.h: Advice for Part (c) Evaluation questions
p: Part (c) questions present an issue where different points of view can be held. 'More than one point of view' often means two opposite views (agree and disagree), but any views that differ are enough.
What the answer needs:
• Well-structured continuous prose in paragraphs.
• Each paragraph states and then considers a point of view or argument.
• Support each view with evidence.
• Do not just describe. Focus on the specific question, not broad themes.
• A firm, clear judgement that follows from the evidence, so the examiner can see the position taken.
• The judgement must be reasoned, not simply stated.
• Use material from across the syllabus for the paper to build arguments and reach a judgement.
The levels-of-response marking grids for AO1 and AO2 are in the specimen mark schemes at www.cambridgeinternational.org/0490 and on the School Support Hub.

b: Point: one view in a clear sentence.
Evidence: a belief, teaching or practice that supports it.
Explain: how it supports the view.
Other view: a different view with its evidence.
Judgement: a reasoned conclusion that answers the question.

sections.h: Assessment objectives and weightings
p: Cambridge tests two assessment objectives (AOs).
• AO1 Knowledge and understanding: demonstrate knowledge and understanding of religious beliefs, practices, teachings and traditions, and how these are linked.
• AO2 Evaluation: evaluate the significance of religious beliefs, practices, teachings and traditions, using evidence and reasoned discussion of different points of view.
Weightings:
• In the whole qualification: AO1 is 60% and AO2 is 40%.
• In each paper: AO1 is 60% and AO2 is 40%.
• In each 20-mark question: parts (a) and (b) give 12 marks for AO1, and part (c) gives 8 marks for AO2. That is the same 60:40 balance.

ex.t: What this means for your teaching
b: Teach knowledge carefully: it is 60% of marks.
Teach evaluation every week, not only before exams: it is 40% of marks.
Use short evaluation tasks from the first term.

sections.h: Command words students must know
p: Command words tell students what to do. The syllabus lists them. Teach each one with an example.
• Assess: make an informed judgement.
• Comment: give an informed opinion.
• Compare: identify or comment on similarities and/or differences.
• Describe: state the points of a topic; give characteristics and main features.
• Discuss: write about issues or topics in depth in a structured way.
• Evaluate: judge or calculate the quality, importance, amount or value of something.
• Explain: set out purposes or reasons; make the relationships between things clear; say why and/or how and support with relevant evidence.
• Give: produce an answer from a given source or recall or memory.
• Identify: name, select or recognise.
• Outline: set out the main points.
• State: express in clear terms.

ex.t: Practice: match the command word to the task
b: 'Identify two features of a synagogue' needs two names.
'Describe one festival' needs main features.
'Explain why' needs reasons with evidence.
'Evaluate' needs different views and a judgement.

units.activity: Make a one-page Syllabus Map. Write: the two religions you will teach and why; the six sections for each religion split across Paper 1 and Paper 2; the paper times and marks; the (a), (b), (c) mark pattern; the AO weightings; and the 11 command words with one example question for each. Share it with a colleague for feedback.

check.q: How many religions do candidates study, and from which?
o: Two from Christianity, Islam and Judaism

check.q: How are the 20 marks in each question shared?
What share of the whole qualification is AO2 Evaluation?
What does 'Evaluate' mean in the command words table?
o: Judge or calculate the quality, importance, amount or value of something
Say what is in a text

units.title: Teaching Religion Fairly: A Respectful Classroom and a First Teaching Plan
units.summary: Build the habits for teaching religion with neutrality, respect and confidence, and write your first plan for Weeks 2 to 6.

sections.h: Teach about religion, not for or against any religion
p: The syllabus asks students to study religion in a social context, with an enquiring and sensitive approach. This means you teach about religions fairly. You do not try to make students believe, or stop believing.
Good habits:
• Use phrases like 'Muslims believe ...', 'Christians teach ...' and 'many Jews practise ...'.
• Describe each religion the way believers describe themselves.
• Present different views inside a religion. Believers do not all think the same.
• Keep your own beliefs out of marking. Give marks for knowledge and reasoning, not agreement.
• Follow your school policy and local law in choosing resources.

b: Say 'according to Christian teaching' instead of 'the truth is'.
Say 'some Muslims believe' when views differ.
Avoid jokes about any belief or believer.
If you are asked what you believe, you may say that your role is to help students understand and evaluate, and bring the class back to the topic.

sections.h: Classroom ground rules
p: Students need to feel safe to ask questions and to disagree politely. Agree rules in the first week and keep them on the wall.
Example rules:
• We listen to every speaker.
• We disagree with ideas, not with people.
• We use respectful words for all beliefs.
• We do not have to share personal beliefs.
• We ask questions with curiosity.
• What is shared in discussion stays in the room, unless someone's safety is at risk.

ex.t: If a student is hurt or offended
b: Stop the discussion calmly.
Remind everyone of the rules.
Speak to the student privately afterwards.
Report anything about safety to the person in charge at school.

sections.h: Handling sensitive topics
p: Religious Studies includes topics such as death, marriage, family roles and social issues. Prepare for these carefully.
Steps:
• Tell parents and school leaders about what you teach, if your school expects it.
• Warn students before a sensitive topic (for example funerals).
• Give students a way to step out quietly if needed.
• Use trusted sources and describe practice factually.
• For evaluation questions, teach students to give reasons for both sides before giving a judgement.
The syllabus says ethical debates on the treatment of animals are not included, and the Cambridge exam is politically neutral.

b: Describe the rite, its meaning and the beliefs about death and afterlife in each chosen religion.
Do not judge any belief.
Give students quiet time to think if they have lost someone.

sections.h: Building your own confidence
p: Many teachers feel less sure about a religion that is not their own. That is normal. A Cambridge teacher keeps learning.
Ways to grow your knowledge:
• Read the syllabus section for each religion slowly, one topic at a time.
• Use trusted textbooks and Cambridge endorsed resources.
• Invite a respectful guest speaker or visit a place of worship, with permission.
• Join the Cambridge forums on the School Support Hub and ask questions.
• Keep a glossary of key words with simple meanings.
• Write answers to past questions yourself and mark them with the levels-of-response grids.

b: Write each new term on a card: word, meaning, example, religion.
Add five new cards each week.
Use the cards for starters and quick quizzes.

sections.h: Your first teaching plan for Weeks 2 to 6
p: Use what you learned in Week 1 to write a one-page plan. The plan will change as you learn more in Weeks 2 to 6.
Include:
• The two religions you will teach, and why.
• Your real teaching hours and weeks.
• A rough order for the six sections (Paper 1 topics then Paper 2 topics, or mixed).
• Evaluation practice every week (AO2 is 40%).
• Past-paper practice and revision time before the exam.
• Support for students who find English or reading hard.
• Access arrangements check at the start.

b: Religions: ___ and ___.
Hours: ___ per week x ___ weeks = ___.
Paper 1 order: worship, beliefs and scriptures, sacred places.
Paper 2 order: festivals and fasts, rites of passage and family, social action.
Review dates: ___.

units.activity: Write your first one-page teaching plan using the template. Then write five ground rules for your class in simple words, and one sentence you will say if a student asks, 'Which religion is true?'. Share it with a colleague and ask for one suggestion.

check.q: What is the best way to describe a religious belief in class?
o: As a fact that everyone must accept
As believers describe it, for example 'Muslims believe ...'

check.q: What should you give marks for in Religious Studies answers?
o: Knowledge and reasoning, not agreement with a belief

check.q: Which of these is a good ground rule?
o: We disagree with ideas, not with people

units.title: Subject Content: How to Read and Use Section 3 of the Syllabus
units.summary: Learn how the content for each religion is organised, what the repeated phrases in the syllabus mean, how to choose your two religions and how to plan your hours.

sections.h: How Section 3 is organised
p: Section 3 of the syllabus is the subject content. It is the list of what students must learn. It has three parts: Christianity, Islam and Judaism. Students study two of the three.
Each religion has six topics, shown with a letter and a number:
• Christianity topics are C1 to C6. Islam topics are I1 to I6. Judaism topics are J1 to J6.
• Paper 1 topics are 1, 2 and 3: Worship; Beliefs and scriptures; Sacred places.
• Paper 2 topics are 4, 5 and 6: Festivals and fasts; Rites of passage and religion and the family; Religion and social action.
• Inside each topic there are numbered sub-topics (for example C1.2) and lettered points (for example C1.2(a)).
• Example: C1.2(d) means Christianity, topic 1 (Worship), sub-topic 2 (key features of church buildings), point (d): the pulpit.

ex.t: Quick map of the six topics (the same for all three religions)
b: 1 Worship: the building, its features, artefacts, public and private worship, leaders.
2 Beliefs and scriptures: the key teachings and the holy book.
3 Sacred places: pilgrimage and places of religious importance.
4 Festivals and fasts: key celebrations, their meaning and how they are kept today.
5 Rites of passage and the family: birth, coming of age, marriage, death, family life, tradition and change.
6 Religion and social action: laws and ethics, love and concern for others, caring for the environment, charities.

sections.h: The repeated phrases and what they ask students to do
p: The syllabus uses the same short phrases again and again. Teach each one, because exam questions are built from them.
• Meaning and importance: say what a feature, object or practice means to believers and why it matters to them.

• Different views / different denominations / different communities: not all believers think or practise the same way. Students must give at least two views, and name who holds them (for example, Catholics, Anglicans, Sunni, Shi'ah, Orthodox Jews, Reform Jews).
• Impact on daily life: how a belief changes what believers do each day (what they eat, how they pray, how they treat others).
• Religious reasons for observing a festival (origins, purpose and symbolism): where it comes from, why it is kept, and what its symbols mean.
• Social significance: what the festival or rite does for families, communities and society (for example, bringing people together, giving to charity, public holidays).
• Different ways it is observed: practice differs between countries, denominations and families.
• Tradition and change: what believers keep from the past, what they change, and how they feel about change.
• Respectful treatment: how believers handle holy books and objects.

ex.t: Example: turning a phrase into a question
b: Syllabus phrase: 'The meaning and importance of the minaret.'
Possible question: 'Explain why the minaret is important in a mosque.'
Answer shape: what it is, what it means (site of light, call to prayer), why believers value it.
Phrase 'different views' might become: 'Some Christians think statues are helpful in worship. Others think they should not be used. Evaluate...'

sections.h: Key words every Religious Studies teacher should be able to define
p: Give these definitions to students in simple words. Each one appears in all three religions in different forms.
• Religion: a system of beliefs and practices about God or the sacred.
• Denomination (Christianity): a group within a religion with its own traditions, for example Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Methodist, Baptist, Pentecostal.
• Tradition: a way of practising a religion that is passed down. In Islam the main traditions are Sunni and Shi'ah. In Judaism, examples are Orthodox, Reform and Liberal.
• Scripture: a holy text. The Bible (Christianity), the Qur'an (Islam) and the Torah (Judaism).
• Artefact: an object used in worship, for example a cross, prayer mat or tallit.
• Ritual: a set pattern of words and actions.
• Rite of passage: a ceremony that marks a key stage of life, such as birth, coming of age, marriage and death.
• Sacrament: in some Christian denominations, a rite believed to give God's grace (for example baptism and the Eucharist).
• Pilgrimage: a journey to a holy place for spiritual reasons.
• Fast: a time of going without food or drink, or some other pleasure, for religious reasons.
• Stewardship: the belief that humans must care for the Earth on behalf of God.

ex.t: Teaching tip: a three-part vocabulary card
b: Front: the word.
Back: a short meaning, one example and one religion it belongs to.
Quiz in pairs for 5 minutes at the start of lessons.

sections.h: Choosing your two religions
p: Students study two religions for both papers. The syllabus does not say which two. The school chooses. Think about these points.
• Teacher knowledge: which religions do you and your colleagues know well, or have training and resources for?
• The community: students may live near mosques, churches or synagogues, or have visitors who can speak respectfully about their faith.
• Resources: are there textbooks, websites and Cambridge endorsed resources for your choices?
• Fairness: students of any belief or none can study any pairing. Their own religion is not a requirement.
• Balance: some topics are similar across religions (pilgrimage, charity, family) which helps students compare.
• Keep the same two religions for Paper 1 and Paper 2 for each student. Candidates answer in two sections of each paper, and the sections must match the religions they studied.
• Consider class size: a very mixed class may need the same two religions taught to all.

ex.t: Example: three common pairings and a note on each
b: Christianity and Islam: many shared figures, such as Ibrahim/Abraham and Jesus/Isa. Good for comparison questions.
Islam and Judaism: shared roots and practices such as dietary laws and charity, and different ways of worshipping.
Christianity and Judaism: shared scriptures in part, and clear differences in beliefs about Jesus.

sections.h: What the syllabus says about resources and sensitivity
p: Section 3 begins with an important message. The syllabus gives you flexibility to design a course that will interest, challenge and engage your students. Where appropriate, you choose the resources and examples. They must be:
• Right for your learners' age.
• Right for their cultural background and learning context.
• In line with your school policies and local legal requirements.
Other points you must know:
• Ethical debates on the treatment of animals are not included. The stewardship topic is about caring for the environment.
• In Judaism, the syllabus writes God as G-d. Students are not penalised for using a different spelling, as long as it is clear which word they mean.
• Cambridge is politically neutral. Do not use materials that push a political view.
• Content removed in 2025 (such as Jihad, Simchat Torah and Shavuot, and the Tenakh, Mishnah and Talmud) must not be taught as exam content, though you may mention them briefly for understanding.

b: Is it accurate according to believers of that religion?
Does it describe, not judge?
Is it suitable for the age and culture of my students?
Is it allowed by my school policy and local law?
Does it match the 2025 to 2027 syllabus?

sections.h: Planning your hours across the six topics
p: Cambridge suggests about 130 guided learning hours for the whole subject. Students study two religions, six topics each, so you have twelve blocks of content to teach plus skills practice.
A simple way to plan:
• About 8 to 10 hours for each of the 12 blocks of content (about 100 to 120 hours).
• About 10 to 15 hours for exam skills: command words, structured answers, evaluation, past papers.
• Revisit key ideas often (spiral approach) instead of teaching a topic once.
• Keep 10 to 14 teaching weeks at the end of the course for revision and timed practice, if your schedule allows.
• Teach evaluation from the start. Part (c) of every question is 8 marks and AO2 is 40% of the grade.

ex.t: Example block plan for one religion (adapt to your hours)
b: Worship (Paper 1): 10 hours.
Beliefs and scriptures: 10 hours.
Sacred places: 6 hours.
Festivals and fasts: 10 hours.
Rites of passage and family: 10 hours.
Religion and social action: 8 hours.

sections.h: A teaching routine that works for every topic
p: Use the same four steps for every sub-topic. This makes planning easier and helps students know what to expect.
• Step 1, Define: teach the key words and what the feature or practice is.
• Step 2, Describe: say how it looks, how it is done, who takes part.
• Step 3, Explain: teach the meaning and why believers value it, with a source such as a teaching from the holy book.
• Step 4, Evaluate: give a question that has different views, so students practise a part (c) answer.
