Add a short quiz at the end of each lesson (three questions). Build a 'different views' table for each topic with columns for viewpoint, who holds it, and reason.

ex.t: Example: the routine for 'the mosque minaret' (Islam I1.2)
b: Define: minaret is the tower of a mosque.
Describe: tall, often with a balcony, where the adhan was traditionally called.
Explain: 'site of light'; it makes the mosque visible and marks it as a place of worship.
Evaluate: 'Minarets are essential for a mosque.' Some Muslims think they are traditional and important; others say the prayer hall matters most.

units.activity: Draw a one-page 'Content Map' for your two chosen religions: write the six topics across the top, and under each write the three most important sub-topics. Next to each sub-topic write one example of 'different views' you can teach. Keep it for planning in Weeks 3 to 6.

check.q: What does the code I2.3 refer to?
o: Islam, topic 2 (Beliefs and scriptures), sub-topic 3 (the Five Pillars)

check.q: Which topics are assessed in Paper 2?
What does 'different views' ask students to do?
o: Give at least two views and say who holds them

units.title: Christianity (C1): Worship in Church, Features, Artefacts, Prayer and Leaders
units.summary: Define, describe and explain how Christians worship: the church, its features and objects, the Eucharist, prayer, use of the Bible and the leaders of the church.

sections.h: C1.1 The church: a building and a people
p: The word 'church' has two meanings. Teach both.
• The church building is a centre for Christian worship and for the Christian community. Christians meet there for services, baptisms, weddings and funerals.
• The church is also the people: the whole community of believers. Many Christians say 'the church is the people, not the building'.
• Different places are called by different names: church, chapel, cathedral, meeting house.
Why it matters:
• The building is a place set apart for prayer and for hearing God's word.
• The community gives support, friendship and shared purpose.

b: 'Explain what is meant by the church.' A church can be a building where Christians worship and also the community of believers. (2 clear points)
Link to evaluation: 'The building is more important than the community.' Some say the building gives a sacred space; others say the people are the real church.

sections.h: C1.2 Key features of church buildings: define and describe
p: The syllabus names these features. Define each, say what it is for, and what it means. Remember that features differ between denominations.

• Altar or holy table: the table at the front. Catholic and Orthodox Christians call it an altar, where the Eucharist is celebrated as a holy sacrifice. Many Protestants call it a holy table or communion table, a place of remembrance.
• Sanctuary: the holy area around the altar. Often raised or marked by rails or steps. It shows the importance of the Eucharist.
• Lectern: a reading stand for the Bible readings. It shows the importance of hearing God's word.
• Pulpit: a raised platform from which the sermon is preached. It shows the importance of teaching.
• Baptistery: a pool large enough for total immersion, used in Baptist and other churches that baptise believers. Font: a container for holy water, used in infant baptism in many churches.
• Representations: statues, images and decorations such as icons, stained glass and paintings. They help worship and teach Bible stories.

• Different views: Catholic and Orthodox churches often have many images and statues. Many Protestant churches have plain walls and few images, because they fear worship of images (see the Second Commandment).

b: Roman Catholic church: altar, sanctuary, statues, candles, crucifix, stained glass, confessional box.
Baptist church: plain interior, pulpit and lectern in the centre, baptistery, simple cross.
Explanation: both focus on God, but they give different importance to sacraments, preaching and images.

sections.h: C1.3 Artefacts used in worship: use, meaning and importance
p: Artefacts are objects used in worship. For each, teach: what it is, how it is used and what it means.
• Copies of the Bible: read in services and private study. It is the word of God for Christians. Treated with respect.

• Cross and crucifix: a cross is the symbol of Jesus' death and resurrection. A crucifix is a cross with the figure of Jesus on it, common among Catholics and Orthodox Christians to remember his suffering. Some Protestants prefer an empty cross to symbolise the resurrection.
• Paten and chalice: the paten is the plate that holds the bread (wafers) and the chalice is the cup for the wine at Communion.
• Missal: a book of prayers and readings used by the Catholic Church for Mass. Book of Common Prayer: used in Anglican worship. Other denominations have their own service books.
• Lectionary: a book of Bible readings for specific days and seasons.

b: Point: the chalice is used at Communion.
Explain: it holds the wine, which represents Jesus' blood.
Link: for many Christians this connects them to the Last Supper and to Jesus' sacrifice.
Different views: for Catholics, the wine becomes the blood of Christ; for many Protestants it is a symbol and a memorial.

sections.h: C1.4 Public (communal) and private worship: describe and explain
p: Public worship is done together in church. Private worship is done alone or at home. Teach both.

• Eucharist (Holy Communion, Mass or the Lord's Supper): Christians share bread and wine in memory of the Last Supper. Key features: readings, prayers, the words of Jesus, sharing the bread and wine. Meaning differs: Catholic and Orthodox Christians believe Christ is truly present; many Protestants see it as a memorial and sign of fellowship.
• Sunday or Sabbath services: most Christians worship on Sunday. Some, such as Seventh-day Adventists, keep Saturday as the Sabbath. A service may include hymns, readings, a sermon and prayers.
• Daily services: some churches (for example Anglican and Catholic) hold daily services such as morning and evening prayer.
• Acts of devotion, confession and reconciliation: for example, confessing sins to a priest in the Catholic Church, or praying for forgiveness in other churches.
• Prayer: thanksgiving (saying thank you), adoration (praising God), intercession (praying for others), petition (asking for oneself) and confession (saying sorry).
• Contemplation and meditation: quiet focus on God, with silence or repeated prayers. Some groups, such as Quakers, worship in silence.
• Bible use and respect: Christians read the Bible in services and private study. They handle it carefully and do not put it on the floor.

ex.t: The Lord's Prayer: content and meaning
b: It begins 'Our Father', showing God as a loving parent to all.
'Hallowed be your name': God's name is holy.
'Your kingdom come, your will be done': a wish that God's rule and goodness spread.
'Give us today our daily bread': asking God to meet our needs.
'Forgive us ... as we forgive': asking forgiveness and promising to forgive others.
'Lead us not into temptation, deliver us from evil': asking for protection.

sections.h: Different views about worship and the Bible
p: Part of C1.4 asks for different views on the role and importance of each form of worship, and on the use of the Bible.
• Sacramental view (Catholic and Orthodox): worship centres on the sacraments, especially the Eucharist, which brings believers close to God.
• Word-centred view (many Protestants): the sermon and Bible reading are central. Communion may be held less often.
• Spirit-led view (Pentecostal and charismatic churches): free prayer, singing, speaking in tongues and healing prayer.
• Quiet view (Quakers and contemplative groups): silent waiting for God.
• On the Bible: some Christians read it literally as God's word. Others read it as inspired but written by people in a historical setting. Both treat it with respect.

ex.t: A part (c) practice question (not an official question)
b: 'Sunday worship in church is the most important part of being a Christian.' Evaluate this statement.
Points for: community, sacraments, hearing the Bible, encouragement.
Points against: faith is lived every day, private prayer is important, some Christians do not attend church.
Judgement: give a reasoned conclusion, for example that Sunday worship is very important but is not the only part of Christian life.

sections.h: C1.5 The roles and significance of leaders
p: Church leaders guide the community in worship and teaching. Teach the main roles.
• The Pope: leader of the Roman Catholic Church, believed by Catholics to be the successor of St Peter. He teaches, guides the Church worldwide and is based in Rome.
• Bishops (in some denominations): oversee a group of churches and ordain priests (for example Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican).
• Priests, ministers, pastors or equivalent: lead worship, preach, administer sacraments, give pastoral care and support families. The title differs by denomination.
• Some denominations have no ordained clergy. For example, Quakers believe all people can speak to God directly and that the Spirit can speak through anyone. Authority is shared in the community.
Reasons for differences:
• Some Christians believe leaders are chosen by God and continue Jesus' apostles.
• Others believe in 'the priesthood of all believers', so no special class of clergy is needed.

b: Roman Catholic: Pope, bishops, priests, deacons.
Baptist: a pastor chosen by the local congregation, with deacons to help.
Quaker meeting: no clergy; people take turns to speak when moved.

sections.h: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
p: Check for these when you mark Christianity Paper 1 answers.
• Treating all Christians as one group. Fix: always name a denomination when a belief or feature differs.
• Mixing up features: pulpit and lectern, font and baptistery, cross and crucifix. Fix: use a labelled diagram and ask students to define each in one line.
• Describing without explaining meaning. Fix: use 'which means...' and 'this is important because...'.
• Giving one view in an evaluation question. Fix: require at least two views plus a judgement.
• Using personal belief. Fix: use phrases like 'Christians believe' and 'some Christians think'.

ex.t: Self-check: can you teach all of C1?
b: I can define the 7 features and 5 artefacts in plain words.
I can describe the Eucharist and name three types of prayer.
I can explain why some denominations have no clergy.
I can write one part (c) question for C1 and plan a reasoned judgement.

units.activity: Make a one-page chart for C1 with three columns: Feature or practice, Meaning and importance, Different views. Fill in at least eight rows (for example altar, pulpit, crucifix, Eucharist, Lord's Prayer, Bible use, Pope, Quaker meeting). Then write one part (c) question and a plan for its answer.

check.q: What is a crucifix?
o: A cross with the figure of Jesus on it

check.q: Which type of prayer is asking God for something for yourself?
Why do some Christian groups have no ordained clergy?
o: They believe all believers can speak to God directly
They have no leaders at all
They do not read the Bible

units.title: Christianity (C2 and C3): Beliefs, the Bible and Places of Pilgrimage
units.summary: Define, describe and explain the Apostles' Creed, the Trinity, Jesus, the Holy Spirit, the Bible, and the places of pilgrimage at Lourdes, Rome, Bethlehem, Nazareth and Jerusalem.

sections.h: C2.1 Christian beliefs about God
p: Teach what Christians believe about God, and how views differ.

• Apostles' Creed: a short statement of Christian belief. It begins 'I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth' and goes on to Jesus, the Holy Spirit, the church, forgiveness and eternal life.
• The Trinity: Christians believe in one God in three persons: Father, Son (Jesus) and Holy Spirit. They are one being. Christians use pictures such as the three-leaf clover to help explain it.
• Non-trinitarian belief: some Christian groups (for example Unitarians and Jehovah's Witnesses) do not accept the Trinity. They believe God is one person.
• The virgin birth: Christians believe Jesus was born to Mary, a virgin, by the power of the Holy Spirit.
• The Incarnation: God taking on human form in Jesus. 'Incarnation' means 'becoming flesh'. Christmas celebrates it.
• Different views: some Christians see the creed as essential and recite it in worship. Others place more weight on the Bible alone.
• Impact on daily life: believing God is loving and present leads to prayer, trust and care for others.

b: 'Outline what Christians believe about the Trinity.' One God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
'Give two reasons the Incarnation matters.' It shows God sharing human life; Jesus can understand human suffering.
Evaluate: 'The Trinity is the most important Christian belief.' Give views and a judgement.

sections.h: C2.2 Christian beliefs about Jesus
p: The Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) are the main source. Teach the story in order and what each part means.

• Birth, suffering, death, resurrection, ascension: Jesus was born in Bethlehem; was arrested, tried and crucified; Christians believe he rose from the dead on the third day and later returned to heaven (ascension). He promised to send the Holy Spirit.

• Salvation and forgiveness: Christians believe Jesus died to save people from sin and offers forgiveness. He is the Messiah ('Chosen One' or Christ). He created the New Covenant: a new relationship between God and people.

• The Last Supper and the Eucharist: Jesus shared bread and wine with his disciples, said they were his body and blood, and told them to do this in memory of him. He washed the disciples' feet to show humble service and predicted his death and betrayal.
• Gethsemane: Jesus prayed in the garden and was arrested after Judas betrayed him. This is the passion (suffering) of Jesus.
• Trials, death and burial: Jesus was tried and sentenced and was crucified and buried.

• Mary, mother of Jesus: honoured by all Christians as the mother of Jesus. Catholics and Orthodox Christians give her special honour and ask for her prayers. Many Protestants honour her but do not pray to her.
• Different views and impact: some focus on the cross (sacrifice), others on the resurrection (new life). Believers try to follow Jesus' example in forgiving and serving.

b: Messiah: the 'chosen one' sent by God.
New Covenant: a new agreement between God and people through Jesus.
Passion: the suffering of Jesus before his death.
Resurrection: Jesus rising from the dead (celebrated at Easter).
Ascension: Jesus going up into heaven.

sections.h: C2.3 Christian beliefs about the Holy Spirit
p: The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity. Christians believe it is the Spirit of God at work on Earth.
• The Spirit of God on Earth: present in the world, in the church and in each believer. Pentecost celebrates the coming of the Spirit on the apostles.
• God's power given to believers: the Spirit gives strength, guidance and courage.
• Fruits of the Spirit: qualities that grow in a believer's life. Galatians 5:22–23 lists love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control.
• Gifts of the Spirit: abilities given for the good of the church. 1 Corinthians 12 lists wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues and interpretation of tongues.
• Different views: Pentecostal and charismatic Christians emphasise gifts like healing and speaking in tongues. Other denominations stress the fruits and the Spirit's quiet guidance.
• Impact on daily life: Christians may pray for the Spirit's help in decisions, and try to show the fruits in daily life.

ex.t: Fruits and gifts: how to remember
b: Fruits: character (how I behave).
Gifts: abilities (what I can do to help others).
Example: patience is a fruit; healing is a gift.

sections.h: C2.4 The Bible: authority, revelation and moral principles
p: The Bible is the holy book of Christians. It has the Old Testament and the New Testament.
• As a source of authority: Christians look to the Bible to know what to believe and how to live. Some believe every word is true. Others believe it needs interpretation.
• As a revelation from God: Christians believe God has shown himself to people through the Bible. 'Revelation' means making known.
• As a source of moral principles: it contains requirements (things Christians should do) and restrictions (things they should not do).
• Ten Commandments (Exodus 20): for example worship only God, honour parents, do not murder, do not steal, do not lie.

• The Beatitudes (Matthew 5): Jesus' blessings on the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, those who seek righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers and those who are persecuted. They teach humility, mercy and peace.
• Importance in Christian life: it shapes worship, prayer, decisions and attitudes to others.

ex.t: Different ways to interpret the Bible
b: Literal: the words mean exactly what they say, including Genesis' creation story as a record of events.
Non-literal: some parts are stories or poems with spiritual meaning.
Both groups use the Bible to guide their lives.
Evaluate: 'The Bible is the only guide Christians need.'

sections.h: C3.1 The importance of pilgrimage for some Christians
p: A pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place. Not all Christians go on pilgrimage, but many find it meaningful.
• Spiritual goals: to grow closer to God, to pray, to seek forgiveness, to ask for healing, to say thank you or to walk where Jesus walked.
• Physical goals: to reach a place, to take part in services, to carry out a promise or a penance.
• Challenges: long journeys, cost, tiredness, illness, crowds. These can strengthen faith or test it.
• Effects on pilgrims: renewed faith, a sense of community with other believers, memories that last, and a changed attitude to life.

b: Question: 'Explain why some Christians go on pilgrimage.'
Point 1: to be close to places linked to Jesus.
Point 2: to ask for healing or comfort.
Point 3: to strengthen faith in a community of pilgrims.

sections.h: C3.2 Places of pilgrimage for Christians
p: Teach each place with: what it is, why it matters, and what pilgrims do.

• Lourdes (France): in 1858 a young girl, Bernadette, said she saw Mary at a grotto. Some Christians go to seek healing and spiritual comfort. Rituals include praying at the Grotto, bathing in the spring water, candlelit processions and Masses.
• Rome (Italy): the burial place of St Peter and the home of the Pope. Pilgrims visit St Peter's Basilica, attend Papal audiences and see the Pope appear in St Peter's Square.

• Bethlehem and Nazareth: Bethlehem is where Jesus was born (Church of the Nativity) and Nazareth is where he grew up (Church of the Annunciation, where the angel told Mary she would have a child, and the Church of St Joseph).

• Jerusalem: the city of Jesus' last days. Pilgrims follow the Way of the Cross (the route Jesus is believed to have walked to crucifixion), visit Gethsemane (where he prayed and was arrested) and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre (built at the traditional sites of his crucifixion and burial).

ex.t: Different views and an evaluation question
b: Some Christians value pilgrimage deeply. Others believe prayer and good deeds at home matter more.
Question: 'Pilgrimage is essential for a strong Christian faith.' Evaluate.
For: strengthens faith, community, shared tradition. Against: not required, expensive, faith can be lived anywhere.
Judgement example: pilgrimage helps many Christians but is not essential.

sections.h: Mini glossary and teaching checklist for C2 and C3
p: Make sure students can define these words quickly:
• Creed, Trinity, Incarnation, virgin birth, Messiah, New Covenant, Eucharist, Last Supper, Gethsemane, resurrection, ascension.
• Holy Spirit, fruits, gifts, revelation, authority, Beatitudes, Ten Commandments.
• Pilgrimage, grotto, basilica, Holy Sepulchre, Way of the Cross.
Teaching checklist:
• Have I taught different views for every belief?
• Have I linked beliefs to daily life with an example?
• Have I included a part (c) task for beliefs and for pilgrimage?
• Have I used respectful language (for example 'Christians believe that Jesus rose')?

b: Give students 12 key words on cards.
They sort them under C2.1, C2.2, C2.3, C2.4 or C3.
They give a one-line meaning for each, then swap and check.

units.activity: Choose one belief from C2 (God, Jesus, the Holy Spirit or the Bible) and one place of pilgrimage from C3. For each write: a definition, a description, an explanation of its meaning and one example of different views. Then write one part (c) question that links both, for example about whether beliefs or pilgrimage matter more.

check.q: What is the Incarnation?
o: The raising of Jesus from the dead
The coming of the Holy Spirit
God taking on human form in Jesus

check.q: Which place do some Christians visit to seek healing and spiritual comfort?
Which list gives two parts of the Bible's moral guidance in the syllabus?
o: The Creed and the Lord's Prayer
The Ten Commandments and the Beatitudes
The Gospels and the Epistles only

units.title: Christianity (C4): Festivals and Fasts
units.summary: Define, describe and explain Easter and Holy Week, Christmas, Epiphany, Ascension, Pentecost, Lent and Advent, with their meaning, social significance and changes today.

sections.h: How to teach each festival (a repeatable pattern)
p: For every festival the syllabus asks the same questions. Use one pattern.
• What is it and when is it? (name, date or season)
• What happened or what does it remember? (the story)
• How is it kept in church and at home? (customs and services)
• Religious reasons: origins, purpose and symbolism.
• Social significance: what it does for families and communities.
• Different ways it is observed: by denomination, country and family.
• Changes today: how practice has changed and how people feel about it.

b: What: 25 December, celebration of Jesus' birth.
Story: Jesus born in Bethlehem (Incarnation).
Church: Midnight Mass, carol services, nativity plays.
Reasons: God coming to Earth; symbols such as the star, crib and light.
Social: gifts, family meals, giving to charity.
Different: Orthodox Christians in some countries celebrate on 7 January.

sections.h: C4.1 Easter and Holy Week
p: Holy Week is the week before Easter. It remembers the last days of Jesus' life. Easter celebrates his resurrection.
• Palm Sunday: remembers Jesus' triumphal entry into Jerusalem when crowds waved palms. Customs: processions and giving out palm crosses. It looks ahead to the end of Holy Week.
• Maundy (Holy) Thursday: remembers the Last Supper and the betrayal in Gethsemane. Customs: Eucharist services and foot-washing, to show humble service.

• Good Friday: remembers the death and crucifixion of Jesus. Customs: services of quiet and reflection, ecumenical witness (Christians of different churches walking or worshipping together) and the Stations of the Cross.
• Holy Saturday: a quiet day of waiting that leads to the Easter Vigil, with the lighting of the Paschal candle and renewal of baptism promises in many churches.
• Easter Sunday: celebrates the resurrection. Customs: sunrise services, processions, joyful hymns and a time of feasting.
• Religious reasons: the resurrection is the centre of Christian belief. It shows victory over death and gives hope of eternal life.
• Social significance: family gatherings, public holidays in many countries, acts of charity, and community processions.
• Different ways: Orthodox churches often celebrate Easter on a different date from Western churches; some churches hold dramatic processions and some hold quiet services.

b: Palm: welcome and victory.
Foot-washing: service and humility.
Cross: sacrifice.
Paschal candle: Christ as the light of the world.
Egg: new life (a popular custom).

sections.h: C4.2 Christmas and C4.3 Epiphany
p: Christmas:
• Celebrates the Incarnation: God becoming human in Jesus.
• Church features: Midnight Mass, carol services, the crib or nativity scene, Advent candles lit to Christmas.
• Religious reasons: Jesus is called the light of the world; the star, angels and manger are symbols of hope and humility.
• Social significance: families meet, gifts are given, charity is increased.
Epiphany (6 January):
• Epiphany means 'revelation': Christ shown to the world.
• It remembers the visit of the Magi (wise men) who brought gold, frankincense and myrrh to the infant Jesus.
• Customs include the King cake and chalking the doors with blessings for the new year.
• Religious reasons: Jesus is revealed to all nations, not only to Jews. Social significance: communal meals and blessing homes.
• Different ways: in some countries, Epiphany is more important than Christmas and gifts are given on that day.

b: Show the route of the Magi from the East.
Link gifts to meaning: gold for kingship, frankincense for worship, myrrh for suffering and death (a common interpretation).
Ask students why a festival for all nations matters.

sections.h: C4.4 Ascension and C4.5 Pentecost
p: Ascension:
• Marks the day Jesus went up into heaven, 40 days after Easter (a Thursday).
• Customs: extinguishing the Paschal candle, processions and an all-night vigil in some churches.
• Religious reasons: Jesus now reigns in heaven and promised to send the Holy Spirit.
• Social significance: in some countries it is a public holiday and a time for family outings.
Pentecost:
• Celebrates the coming of the Holy Spirit on the twelve apostles, 50 days after Easter. Acts 2 describes tongues of fire, a rush of wind and speaking in different languages.
• Customs: wearing red (the colour of fire), Kneeling Prayers services, special hymns.
• Religious reasons: often called the 'birthday of the church'. The Spirit gave the apostles courage to spread the message.
• Different ways: Pentecostal churches give great weight to the Spirit; others hold quiet services.

b: Ascension: Jesus leaves the earth; promise of the Spirit.
Pentecost: Spirit arrives; the church begins to spread.
Symbols: Paschal candle extinguished (Ascension), red robes and fire (Pentecost).

sections.h: C4.6 Lent and C4.7 Advent: seasons of preparation
p: Lent:
• A time of 40 days before Easter, remembering Jesus' 40 days in the wilderness. Preparation for Easter.
• A time of fasting and giving up luxuries, money or time in service of others.
• Marked in churches by services on Ash Wednesday, when ashes in the shape of a cross are placed on foreheads as a sign of sorrow for sin.
• Social significance: charity appeals, shared meals, community study groups.
Advent:
• The four weeks before Christmas. Preparation for both Jesus' birth and the Second Coming (his return).
• A time of fasting, prayer and charity.
• Marked by Advent services, an Advent wreath with four candles lit week by week, and Advent calendars.
• Different ways: some Christians fast strictly, others use it for prayer and giving.

b: To focus on God.
To remember Jesus' sacrifice.
To show self-discipline.
To remember the poor and give what is saved to charity.

sections.h: C4.8 Changes to festivals and fasts
p: Teach how practice has changed in the modern world.
• Changes in traditional practice: fewer people fast strictly; many take part in cultural traditions without church; some churches hold online services or family-friendly services.
• Commercial aspects: Christmas and Easter are linked to shopping, gifts, chocolate eggs and holidays in some countries.
• Different Christian feelings: some welcome the joy and giving. Others worry that the religious meaning is lost and that spending is too important.
• Teach students to give both views and a reasoned judgement.

b: 'Christmas has lost its true meaning.' Evaluate this statement.
For: shopping and gifts dominate, many people do not attend church.
Against: churches are full at Christmas, charity increases, family time is valued.
Judgement: you might conclude that the meaning has changed for some but remains strong for many believers.

sections.h: Quick revision table and common mistakes
p: Use this table to help students revise.
• Festival | Date or season | Main meaning | One custom.
• Palm Sunday | before Easter | entry into Jerusalem | palm crosses.
• Maundy Thursday | Holy Week | Last Supper | foot-washing.
• Good Friday | Holy Week | crucifixion | Stations of the Cross.
• Easter | spring | resurrection | sunrise service.
• Christmas | 25 December | Incarnation | Midnight Mass.
• Epiphany | 6 January | revelation to the world | King cake.
• Ascension | 40 days after Easter | Jesus goes to heaven | extinguishing the Paschal candle.
• Pentecost | 50 days after Easter | coming of the Spirit | wearing red.
Common mistakes: confusing Ascension and Pentecost, saying Lent is only about chocolate, and describing customs without meaning.

b: I can state the meaning of each festival in one sentence.
I can explain one symbol for each.
I can give one social significance and one change today.
I can write a part (c) answer with two views.

units.activity: Make a one-page 'Festival Wheel' with the eight Christian festivals and seasons from C4. For each write the date or season, the meaning, one custom and one symbol. Then write a part (c) question about changes (for example commercialisation) with two views.

check.q: What does Epiphany celebrate?
o: The revelation of Christ to the world, linked to the visit of the Magi
The coming of the Holy Spirit

check.q: Which festival remembers Jesus going up into heaven?
What happens on Ash Wednesday?
o: Ashes are placed on foreheads in the shape of a cross to show sorrow for sin

units.title: Christianity (C5 and C6): Rites of Passage, Family and Social Action
units.summary: Define, describe and explain baptism, confirmation, marriage and funerals, Christian family teachings, tradition and change, love and concern for others, stewardship and charities.

sections.h: C5.1 Baptism
p: Baptism is the rite by which a person becomes part of the Christian community. Different denominations baptise differently.

• Infant baptism: babies are baptised, often with water poured over the head in the church, in Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Methodist and other churches. Parents and godparents promise to bring the child up in the faith.

• Adult (believers') baptism: people who choose to follow Jesus are baptised, often by full immersion in a pool, in Baptist and many other churches. Some churches use a dedication service for babies instead, then baptism when the child chooses faith.
• Godparents and sponsors: promise to help the child grow in faith and pray for them.

• Rituals and meaning: water (washing away sin and new life), signing with the cross, anointing with oil in some churches, a candle (the light of Christ), a white garment (purity), the words 'I baptise you in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit'.
• Importance: baptism shows belonging, forgiveness and new life with God.

b: Infant baptism: parents decide, community promises, child's faith grows later.
Believers' baptism: the person decides, faith is declared in public.
Evaluate: 'Baptism should only be for people who choose it themselves.' Give views and a judgement.

sections.h: C5.2 Coming of age: confirmation and First Communion
p: Coming of age ceremonies mark growing in faith and taking responsibility.

• Confirmation: in churches that baptise infants, such as Catholic, Anglican and Orthodox traditions, young people confirm for themselves the promises made at baptism. A bishop or priest lays hands on them and prays for the Holy Spirit. A sponsor supports them.
• First Communion: in some denominations, children receive the Eucharist for the first time, often wearing white and after special lessons.
• Rituals and meaning: affirming belief, prayers, anointing with oil (in some traditions), the laying on of hands and receiving the bread and wine.
• Importance of becoming a full member: they can take full part in worship and make adult decisions about faith.

b: It shows the person's own faith.
It gives the support of the church community.
It marks the move from child to responsible believer.

sections.h: C5.3 and C5.4 Marriage and funeral rites
p: Marriage:
• A marriage ceremony takes place in church with or without a Eucharist (Communion).

• Vows: promises of love and faithfulness 'for better, for worse, till death us do part'. Rings are exchanged, as a sign of unending love. In Orthodox weddings, couples wear crowns to show they are kings and queens of a new household.
• In some denominations (Catholic and Orthodox), marriage is a sacrament, a sign of God's grace.
Funeral rites:
• The Last Rites: in Catholic and Orthodox churches, a priest prepares a dying person with prayers, confession and anointing. It is a sacrament.
• Funeral service: prayers, readings, hymns and a sermon of comfort. Burial (interment) or cremation, with prayers and blessings.
• Significance: acknowledges death, commits the person to God, supports the bereaved and expresses hope of eternal life.

ex.t: Different views on marriage and funerals
b: Sacrament (Catholic and Orthodox): marriage joins two people with God's blessing for life.
Covenant or promise (many Protestants): a serious public promise before God.
Cremation is accepted by many Christians; some prefer burial for respect.

sections.h: C5.5 and C5.6 The family and tradition and change
p: The family is central in Christian teaching.
• Roles and responsibilities of men and women: traditional teaching describes husbands as heads and wives as helpers, but many Christians now stress equality and partnership.
• Nurture of the young: parents should teach faith, give love and discipline, and bring children to church.
• Care of the elderly: honour parents (Fifth Commandment) and care for older relatives.

• Marriage, divorce and remarriage: Roman Catholics teach marriage is for life, so divorce is not recognised, though marriages can be annulled. Orthodox and many Protestant churches allow divorce and remarriage in some situations. Different views are important.

• Tradition and change: some communities keep traditional roles, believing they follow the Bible. Others support change, such as women priests or equal roles. Social change can bring emotional and spiritual challenges, for example when family members disagree.

b: 'Christian families should keep traditional roles.' Evaluate.
For: scripture, stability, shared values.
Against: equality, modern life, different families.
Judgement: give a reasoned conclusion.

sections.h: C6.1 and C6.2 Concern for others and stewardship of the environment
p: Concern for others:
• Agape: unconditional, selfless love as shown in the Gospels, for example the Good Samaritan.
• The Two Greatest Commandments: Jesus taught that the greatest commandments are to love God with all your heart and to love your neighbour as yourself (Matthew 22).
• Service: giving time, work and money, for example volunteering, giving to the poor, visiting the sick.
Stewardship of the environment:
• Humans are stewards (caretakers) of the Earth for God.
• God created everything, and people have a duty to care for creation. Christians may recycle, reduce waste, plant trees and campaign for the environment.
• The syllabus note: the focus is stewardship of the environment, not debates on how animals are treated.

b: A church recycling scheme or 'green church' award.
A food bank run by a congregation.
A prayer for creation at services.

sections.h: C6.3 Christian organisations that relieve poverty
p: Teach what each organisation does, and why Christians support them.
• Tearfund: a Christian charity that works to relieve poverty, support communities and respond to disasters, motivated by Christian faith.
• Caritas: the international Catholic charity network, helping with poverty, health, disasters and justice.
• Christian Aid: works with partners worldwide against poverty and for justice.
• Groups particular to your country: local church food banks, clinics, schools and relief funds that support the community. Teach at least one from your own context.
• Spiritual as well as physical needs: many groups offer prayer and pastoral care as well as food and shelter.

• Missionary activity and charity work: Christians believe Jesus taught them to help others and to share the good news. Their charity is motivated by faith, for example 'I was hungry and you gave me food' (Matthew 25).

b: 'Christian charities should only help Christians.' Evaluate.
Views: Christians are called to help everyone; some groups also seek to share faith.
Judgement: most major charities help people of all beliefs, motivated by love of neighbour.

sections.h: Revision checklist and common mistakes
p: Check that students can do all of the following.
• Explain two types of baptism and name two rituals.
• Explain confirmation and First Communion.
• Describe a church wedding and a funeral.
• Give two Christian views on divorce.
• Define agape, stewardship and the Two Greatest Commandments.
• Name three Christian charities and say what one of them does.
Common mistakes: saying all Christians baptise babies; forgetting different views on marriage; naming charities without saying what they do; ignoring the syllabus note on animals.

b: Name one rite of passage and its meaning.
Give two views on one Christian family teaching.
State one way a Christian charity shows love of neighbour.

units.activity: For C5 and C6 make a table with columns: Topic, What happens or what is taught, Meaning, Different views. Include baptism, confirmation, marriage, funeral, family roles, divorce, agape, stewardship and two charities. Then write one part (b) explanation and one part (c) evaluation question and plan answers.

check.q: What is believers' baptism?
o: Baptism of someone who chooses faith, often by full immersion

check.q: What are the Two Greatest Commandments?
o: Love God and love your neighbour
Do not steal and do not lie
Go to church and give money

check.q: Which is a Christian organisation that relieves poverty named in the syllabus?

units.title: Islam (I1): Worship in the Mosque, Prayer, the Qur'an and Leaders
units.summary: Define, describe and explain the mosque and its features, the artefacts of prayer, the adhan, wudu, salah, Jumu'ah, du'a, dhikr, respect for the Qur'an, and the imam and mu'azzin.

sections.h: I1.1 The mosque: centre for worship and for the ummah
p: Teach the key terms and why the mosque matters.
• Mosque (masjid): means 'place of prostration'. It is a centre for Muslim worship, where Muslims pray together.
• Ummah: the worldwide community of Muslims. The mosque is the centre of the ummah in a local area.
• Besides prayer, mosques often host Qur'an classes, community events, advice, charity collections and celebrations such as Eid.
• Any clean place can be used for prayer, but the mosque brings the community together, especially on Fridays.

b: 'State what is meant by masjid.' It means 'place of prostration' and is the Muslim place of worship.
Part (c) link: 'The mosque is the most important place for a Muslim.' Views: community, prayer, learning; against: prayer can be anywhere, faith lived daily.

sections.h: I1.2 Key features of a mosque: define, describe and explain
p: Each feature has a purpose and a meaning. Practices differ in different Muslim communities.
• Minaret ('site of light'): the tower of the mosque. Traditionally the adhan was called from it. It marks the mosque.
• Dome: symbolises the vault of heaven. It also helps the sound of prayers carry.
• Qiblah: the direction of Makkah, which Muslims face to pray.
• Mihrab: a niche in the qiblah wall that shows the direction of prayer.
• Minbar: a stepped platform from which the imam gives the Friday sermon.
• Musalla (prayer hall): the main room where people pray. It is carpeted, often with lines to help people line up.

• Separate areas for men and women: many mosques have separate spaces so that people can pray without distraction and with modesty. Some mosques have a balcony or a different room for women. Views differ about how the spaces are arranged.

• Architecture and calligraphy: mosques use geometric patterns and Arabic calligraphy of Qur'an verses. There are no pictures or statues of humans or animals because Muslims believe only God should be worshipped and images could lead to idol worship.

b: Some mosques are large with domes and minarets; others are simple rooms.
Styles vary by country: Ottoman, Mughal, West African mud-brick mosques.
Features differ, but all face the qiblah.

sections.h: I1.3 Artefacts used in worship
p: Teach what each object is, how it is used and what it means.
• Copies of the Qur'an: the holy book, kept in a clean place and handled with care. Often placed on a stand (rehal).
• Compass: shows the direction of the qiblah, useful in travel or in buildings with no mihrab.
• Prayer mat (sajjadah): a clean place to pray. Often has a niche design that points to Makkah.
• Turbah (prayer stone): a small tablet of clay on which the forehead rests in prostration, used mostly by Shi'ah Muslims, because it comes from the earth.
• Misbahah (prayer beads, tasbih): used for dhikr, counting the repeated praise of God (often 33 times for each phrase).

b: Describe: a prayer mat is a rug used for prayer.
Explain: it keeps the place clean and helps Muslims focus on worship.
Different views: not all Muslims use a turbah; Sunni Muslims often pray on carpets or mats.

sections.h: I1.4 Public and private worship: adhan, wudu and salah
p: These are central to Muslim daily life.

• Adhan (call to prayer): called by the mu'azzin before each prayer. It announces the time and invites people to worship. It begins 'Allahu Akbar' (God is greatest). It is also whispered into a newborn baby's ear.
• Wudu (ablution): washing the hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head and feet before prayer. It shows purity and readiness to meet God.
• Salah (formal prayer) and the five prayer times: Fajr (dawn), Dhuhr (midday), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (sunset), Isha (night).

• Rak'ahs: units of prayer, a set sequence of movements: standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting, with recitation of the Qur'an and praise of God. The number of rak'ahs varies by prayer (for example Fajr has 2, Maghrib has 3, others have 4).
• Significance: the movements show humility and submission to God. Praying together builds unity.

ex.t: Order of salah in simple words
b: Intention and takbir (raising hands, 'Allahu Akbar').
Standing: reciting Surah al-Fatihah and another passage.
Bowing (ruku), standing again, prostration (sujud).
Sitting and ending with greetings of peace.

sections.h: Jumu'ah, du'a and dhikr
p: More forms of worship the syllabus names.

• Jumu'ah prayer (Friday midday prayer): the most important weekly prayer, prayed at the mosque with a sermon (khutbah). Muslim men are required to attend; women may attend. It brings the community together.
• Du'a (private prayer): personal asking and speaking to God in one's own words, often with raised hands, before or after salah, with preparation such as wudu and praising God.

• Dhikr (remembrance): repeating names or phrases of God, for example 'SubhanAllah', 'Alhamdulillah', 'Allahu Akbar', often with prayer beads. It is a devotional practice that brings calm and closeness to God.
• Different views: some Muslims, especially Sufi groups, place great weight on dhikr and use it in group gatherings. Others value it as a personal practice.

b: Public: salah and Jumu'ah with the community, led by the imam.
Private: du'a and dhikr alone or at home.
Evaluate: 'Private prayer is more important than public worship.' Give views and a judgement.

sections.h: The Qur'an in worship and respect for it
p: The Qur'an is the holy book of Islam. Muslims believe it is God's word as revealed to Prophet Muhammad (pbuh).
• Use in public worship: recited in salah, in the Friday sermon and during Ramadan.
• Use in private prayer and study: read, memorised and studied at home and in classes.
• Different views: some Muslims stress recitation in Arabic; others emphasise understanding translated meanings. Some memorise the whole Qur'an (hafiz).
• Respectful treatment: wash (wudu) before touching it, keep it clean and in a high place, never on the floor, wrap it in cloth, do not touch it with unclean hands, and do not put other items on top.

ex.t: Explain why Muslims treat the Qur'an with respect
b: It is the word of God.
It guides every part of life.
Respect shows love for God and obedience.

sections.h: I1.5 Leaders: the imam and the mu'azzin
p: Islam has no priesthood, but there are leaders in the mosque.

• Imam: a Muslim religious leader. He leads the prayers, delivers the Friday sermon, teaches the Qur'an, advises families and officiates at weddings and funerals. He is often chosen for knowledge and character.
• Mu'azzin (muezzin): the person who gives the call to prayer (adhan). Many mosques now use recordings or loudspeakers.
• In Shi'ah communities, imam can also have a special meaning for the descendants of Ali (see I2.5).
• Different views: some communities have a paid imam; in others, a respected member leads prayer.

b: Explain the role of the imam in the mosque.
He leads prayer; gives the khutbah; teaches; supports families; leads at marriage and funerals.
Link: this shows the mosque as a community centre.

sections.h: Revision and common mistakes
p: Common mistakes to look for.
• Confusing the imam and the mu'azzin.
• Saying the minaret is where Muslims pray, instead of where the adhan was called.
• Forgetting qiblah is the direction of Makkah.
• Writing 'Allah' as a different god from the God of other religions. Use 'God (Allah)'.
• Describing prayer without explaining meaning.
Revision tasks:
• Draw and label a mosque plan with qiblah, mihrab, minbar and musalla.
• List the five prayers with times.
• Write three sentences on respect for the Qur'an.

b: I can define 10 words from I1.
I can describe wudu and salah in order.
I can explain why there are no images in mosques.
I can write a part (c) question on public and private worship.

units.activity: Make a labelled mosque plan with minaret, dome, qiblah wall, mihrab, minbar and musalla. Beside it write a one-line meaning for each feature. Then write a part (b) answer on 'Explain the importance of salah for Muslims' using at least three points.

check.q: What is the qiblah?
o: The direction of Makkah that Muslims face in prayer

check.q: Who gives the call to prayer?
Which prayer is Friday midday prayer?

units.title: Islam (I2 and I3): Beliefs, Prophet Muhammad, Sunni and Shi'ah, Hajj and Umrah
units.summary: Define, describe and explain the Six Articles of Faith, the five roots of Usul ad-Din, the Five Pillars, the life of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh), Sunni and Shi'ah origins, the Qur'an, and the places and rites of Hajj and Umrah.

sections.h: I2.1 The Six Articles of Faith
p: These are the basic beliefs of Sunni Muslims (and shared by Shi'ah with different emphasis).
• Tawhid: the oneness of God. God is one, with no partners. The most important belief.
• Risalah: belief in prophets sent by God to guide humanity, such as Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad (pbuh).
• Akhirah: life after death. People will be judged by God on the Day of Judgement and will go to Paradise or Hell.
• Mala'ikah: belief in angels, God's servants such as Jibril who brought revelation.
• Qadar: predestination, that God knows and has power over all things. Muslims also believe humans have free will and responsibility.
• Kutub: God's holy books, including the Torah, Psalms, Gospel and the Qur'an, the final book.
• Different views and impact: Muslims may differ on how they understand Qadar and free will. Belief in akhirah shapes honesty, prayer and care for others.

b: 'Outline the Muslim belief in tawhid.' God is one and has no partners.
Link to daily life: Muslims worship only God and avoid idol worship.
Evaluate: 'Tawhid is the most important belief in Islam.' Views and judgement.

sections.h: I2.2 The five roots of Usul ad-Din (Shi'ah)
p: This is a new topic in the 2025 to 2027 syllabus. These are the five basic beliefs in Shi'ah Islam.
• Tawhid: oneness of God.
• 'Adl: divine justice. God is always fair and just.
• Risalah (also called Nubuwwah): prophets.
• Imamah: the authority of the imams, the leaders from the family of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) chosen by God, beginning with Ali.
• Mi'ad: the Day of Resurrection, when all people are raised for judgement.
• Different views: Sunni Muslims do not hold Imamah as a root of religion. Shi'ah consider it essential.
• Impact on daily life: belief in God's justice encourages fairness; belief in the imams guides Shi'ah in religious knowledge and practice.

ex.t: Compare Six Articles and Five Roots
b: Shared: tawhid, prophets, life after death.
Different: Sunni list includes angels, holy books and qadar; the Shi'ah roots include divine justice and imamah.
Teach this carefully and without judging either group.

sections.h: I2.3 The Five Pillars of Islam
p: The Five Pillars are the main acts of worship all Muslims try to follow.
• Shahadah: the declaration of faith: 'There is no god but God and Muhammad is the messenger of God.' Saying it with sincerity makes a person Muslim.
• Salah: prayer five times a day.
• Sawm: fasting during the month of Ramadan.
• Zakah: obligatory charity, usually 2.5% of savings above a minimum amount, given to people in need.
• Hajj: pilgrimage to Makkah once in a lifetime for those who are able.
• Different views: Shi'ah Muslims also teach the Ten Practices of the religion (Furu' ad-Din), which include the five pillars with other duties.
• Impact on daily life: they give discipline, community, generosity and closeness to God.

b: 'Explain the importance of the Five Pillars for Muslims.'
Give at least three points with explanation, such as unity, discipline and obedience to God.
Add an example: fasting in Ramadan shows self-control and empathy for the poor.

sections.h: I2.4 Prophet Muhammad (pbuh)
p: Teach the life in order, with the key events and their importance.
• Early life: born in Makkah around 570 CE, orphaned young, known as al-Amin (the trustworthy) for his honesty.

• First revelation: around 610 CE, in the cave of Hira', the angel Jibril brought the first words of the Qur'an ('Read!'). Muhammad (pbuh) was frightened but was comforted by his wife Khadijah. This marks the start of prophethood.
• Persecution: when he preached the oneness of God and equality, the leaders of Makkah opposed him, because it challenged their idols, trade and power. Early Muslims were persecuted.
• Hijrah: the flight to Madinah in 622 CE. It is the start of the Islamic calendar. There he formed the first Muslim community.
• Final messenger and Seal of the Prophets: Muslims believe he is the last prophet and that the Qur'an is the final revelation.

ex.t: Why does the hijrah matter today?
b: It marks the start of the Muslim calendar.
It shows patience, faith and sacrifice.
It established the first Muslim community.

sections.h: I2.5 and I2.6 Sunni and Shi'ah origins; the Qur'an
p: Teach respectfully and factually.
• After the death of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) in 632 CE, Muslims disagreed on who should lead.
• Sunni: believe the community chose Abu Bakr as the first caliph, followed by 'Umar and 'Uthman. They respect the early caliphs.
• Shi'ah: believe the Prophet chose his cousin and son-in-law Ali as leader, and that leadership belongs to the Prophet's family. They teach the Twelve Imams, descendants of Ali.
• The Qur'an: seen as the final revelation and authority, and a source of moral principles.

• Requirements and restrictions: Surah Al-An'am 6:151–153 and Surah Al-Isra' 17:23–39 teach, for example, worship God alone, be kind to parents, do not kill unjustly, do not commit adultery, give full measure, keep promises, and care for orphans.
• Interpretation: some Muslims stress literal meaning; others use scholarship and context. All agree on the Qur'an's authority.

ex.t: Compare Sunni and Shi'ah in a short table
b: Leadership after Muhammad (pbuh): Abu Bakr and the caliphs (Sunni) | Ali and the imams (Shi'ah).
Number of imams in the main Shi'ah tradition taught here: twelve.
Both: follow the Qur'an, the Five Pillars and the Prophet's example.

sections.h: I3.1 and I3.2 Hajj: the importance and the performance
p: Hajj is the pilgrimage to Makkah. It takes place in the month of Dhu al-Hijjah.
• Goals: spiritual (forgiveness, closeness to God, equality) and physical (completing the rites).
• Challenges: heat, crowds, tiredness, cost. They test patience and faith.
• Stages and places (as in the syllabus):
• Ihram: pilgrims wear simple white clothes (men) or modest dress (women) to show equality and purity.

• Makkah and the Ka'bah: the cube-shaped building at the heart of the Sacred Mosque. Pilgrims walk around it seven times (tawaf) and walk between the hills of Safa and Marwa (sa'y), remembering Hajar's search for water for her son Isma'il.
• The well of Zamzam: the miraculous water that appeared for Hajar and Isma'il; pilgrims drink from it.
• Mina: pilgrims stay in tents and throw pebbles at pillars (stoning), recalling Ibrahim's rejection of temptation.
• 'Arafat: the most important day. Pilgrims stand on the plain praying and asking for forgiveness. Mount of Mercy (Jabal Rahmah) is a hill on the plain.
• Muzdalifah: pilgrims spend the night under the open sky and collect pebbles.

ex.t: Order of the main Hajj rites (a simple outline)
b: Enter ihram and go to Makkah for tawaf.
Travel to Mina, then 'Arafat for the day of standing.
Night at Muzdalifah, then stoning at Mina.
Sacrifice, shaving or cutting hair, final tawaf and sa'y.
End: Eid al-Adha is celebrated.

sections.h: I3.3 and I3.4 'Umrah, Makkah and Madinah
p: 'Umrah and the two cities.
• 'Umrah: the 'lesser pilgrimage'. It can be done at any time of the year.
• Similarities with Hajj: wearing ihram, tawaf around the Ka'bah and sa'y between Safa and Marwa.
• Differences: 'Umrah is shorter, is not compulsory, and does not include 'Arafat, Muzdalifah or stoning. Hajj is one of the Five Pillars.
• Makkah: birthplace of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh), where early Muslims were persecuted and from where the hijrah began.
• Madinah: destination of the hijrah; the first Muslim community was established there; the site of the first mosque; and the place where Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) died and is buried.

b: 'Hajj is more important than any other Pillar.' Evaluate.
For: only done once, tests everything, unites Muslims worldwide.
Against: shahadah is the foundation; salah is daily; not everyone can afford Hajj.
Judgement: reasoned conclusion with evidence.

sections.h: Revision and common mistakes
p: Common mistakes.
• Mixing up the Five Pillars with the Six Articles.
• Treating the five roots of Usul ad-Din as the same as the Five Pillars.
• Saying Hajj happens in Ramadan. It happens in Dhu al-Hijjah.
• Confusing Hajj and 'Umrah.
• Presenting Sunni and Shi'ah as unfriendly or in conflict instead of as two traditions with different history.
Revision tasks:
• Make a three-column table: Six Articles | Five Roots | Five Pillars.
• Draw a Hajj map with Makkah, Mina, Muzdalifah, 'Arafat.
• Write two evaluation points for and against the statement above.

b: I can list the Six Articles, Five Roots and Five Pillars.
I can explain the hijrah and its importance.
I can explain two differences between Sunni and Shi'ah views on leadership.
I can describe the Hajj rites in order.

units.activity: Make a poster that compares the Six Articles of Faith, the five roots of Usul ad-Din and the Five Pillars. Under it add a timeline of Prophet Muhammad's life with five events. Finally, write a part (c) answer plan on whether Hajj is the most important Pillar.

check.q: Which belief is the oneness of God?
Which new topic was added to the Islam content in 2025?
o: The five roots of Usul ad-Din

check.q: What is the hijrah?
o: The flight of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) and early Muslims from Makkah to Madinah

units.title: Islam (I4): Eid al-Adha, Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr
units.summary: Define, describe and explain 'Id al-Adha, the fast of Ramadan including iftar, suhur, i'tikaf and Laylat al-Qadr, 'Id al-Fitr, and how festivals and fasts are changing today.

sections.h: Teach each festival with one pattern
p: Use the same questions for each festival and fast.
• What is it, and when is it? (Islamic calendar is lunar, so dates move about 10 to 11 days earlier each year.)
• What does it remember?
• How is it kept (customs, food, prayer)?
• Religious reasons: origins, purpose and symbolism.
• Social significance.
• Different ways it is observed.
• Changes and different feelings today.

b: Ramadan: ninth month of the Islamic calendar.
'Id al-Fitr: the first day of Shawwal, the month after Ramadan.
'Id al-Adha: the tenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah, the month of Hajj.

sections.h: I4.1 'Id al-Adha (feast of sacrifice)
p: 'Id al-Adha is one of the two main festivals.
• It is the celebration at the end of Hajj, kept by Muslims all over the world.
• Connection to Ibrahim (AS): Muslims remember God's testing of Ibrahim, who was ready to sacrifice his son. God provided a ram instead. It shows complete trust and obedience.
• Importance of sacrifice in Muslim life: giving up something valued for God and for others.

• Customs: special 'Id prayer at the mosque or open ground, wearing best clothes, greeting 'Id Mubarak', sacrificing an animal for those who can afford it, and sharing the meat in three parts: for the family, for relatives and friends, and for the poor.
• Religious reasons: obedience, trust, sacrifice and thankfulness.
• Social significance: sharing food, visiting family, helping the poor.
• Different ways: customs vary by country, such as the type of animal and the dishes cooked; some give money to charities to buy and distribute the meat.

b: Point: 'Id al-Adha remembers Ibrahim's willingness to obey God.
Explain: this teaches trust and sacrifice.
Link: Muslims share meat with the poor to show care for the community.

sections.h: I4.2 The fast of Ramadan: rules and benefits
p: Ramadan is the month of fasting. It is one of the Five Pillars (sawm). It is the month in which the Qur'an was first revealed.
• Rules: fast from dawn to sunset. No eating, drinking, smoking or marital relations during the day. Avoid bad speech and behaviour.
• Exemptions: children, the elderly, the sick, travellers, pregnant or nursing women and women who are menstruating are not required to fast.
• Compensations: missed days are made up later, or people who cannot fast give food to a poor person (fidyah). Deliberately breaking a fast needs a larger penalty.
• Spiritual benefits: self-control, thankfulness, empathy for the poor, closeness to God and a fresh start.
• Iftar: the meal to break the fast at sunset, often beginning with dates and water, then prayer and a shared meal. Physically, it restores energy; spiritually, it shows gratitude and fellowship.
• Suhur: the pre-dawn meal. It gives strength for the day and follows the Prophet's example.
• Purpose for the individual and the ummah: personal discipline and unity, as Muslims all over the world fast together.

b: Saying everyone must fast. Exemptions exist.
Saying fasting is only about food. It includes behaviour and prayer.
Forgetting that dates vary because of the lunar calendar.

sections.h: I4.2 continued: i'tikaf, Laylat al-Qadr and giving
p: The last ten days of Ramadan are especially important.
• I'tikaf: a spiritual retreat in the mosque during the last ten days of Ramadan. Muslims spend time in prayer, Qur'an reading and remembrance, with little talk of worldly matters.

• Laylat al-Qadr (Night of Power): the night the Qur'an was first revealed. It is believed to be one of the odd nights in the last ten days, often the 27th. The Qur'an says it is better than a thousand months. Muslims pray, recite the Qur'an and ask forgiveness.
• Sadaqah: voluntary giving. Muslims give more in Ramadan, and also pay zakat al-Fitr, a small donation for the poor before the 'Id prayer. Giving shows concern and gratitude.
• Religious reasons for observing Ramadan: obedience to God, learning discipline, remembering the revelation.
• Social significance: family and community iftars, charity drives, a sense of belonging.
• Different ways: some communities have long evening prayers (tarawih); some pray at home; patterns of food and gatherings differ by country.

b: 'The most important benefit of fasting is spiritual.' Evaluate.
For: self-control, closeness to God, gratitude.
Against: the social benefits of unity and charity also matter; fasting has health aspects.
Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.

sections.h: I4.3 'Id al-Fitr (the end of Ramadan)
p: 'Id al-Fitr means 'the festival of breaking the fast'.
• It celebrates the end of Ramadan. It starts when the new moon of Shawwal is seen.

• Features: special 'Id prayers in congregation, greetings such as 'Id Mubarak, special food prepared and shared with family and friends, wearing new or best clothes, community celebrations, presents (especially for children) and charity (zakat al-Fitr).
• Religious reasons: thanking God for the strength to fast, celebrating completing Ramadan, and sharing joy with the whole community.
• Social significance: families reunite, neighbours are visited, the poor are included.
• Different ways: sweets and dishes vary around the world; some communities hold large fairs, others small gatherings.

b: 'Id al-Fitr: end of Ramadan; thanks; sweets and gifts.
'Id al-Adha: end of Hajj; sacrifice; sharing meat.
Both: special 'Id prayer, new clothes, visiting family, charity.

sections.h: I4.4 Changes to festivals and fasts
p: Teach how practice is changing and why people feel differently.

• Changes in the modern world: shift work and school times affect fasting; online iftars and Qur'an classes; moon sighting by astronomy or by eye (different communities follow different methods); commercial 'Id markets.
• Different views: some Muslims welcome changes that help people take part. Others want to keep traditional methods, for example moon sighting by eye.
• Feelings: some worry that festivals are becoming too commercial or that tradition is lost; others see change as a way to keep the faith alive.

b: 'Ramadan is too difficult to keep in the modern world.' Evaluate.
For: long hours at work or school, hot climates, health.
Against: exemptions exist, community support, deep spiritual value.
Judgement: reasoned.

sections.h: Revision table and common mistakes
p: Revision table:
• 'Id al-Adha | 10 Dhu al-Hijjah | Ibrahim's trust and sacrifice | animal sacrifice and sharing meat.
• Ramadan | 9th month | revelation of the Qur'an | fasting, iftar, suhur.
• Laylat al-Qadr | last ten nights | first revelation | night prayers.
• 'Id al-Fitr | 1 Shawwal | end of fast | 'Id prayers and zakat al-Fitr.
Common mistakes: mixing the two Eids; forgetting exemptions and compensations; ignoring the social significance; saying fasting is only about hunger.

b: Name one custom for each Eid.
Give two exemptions from fasting.
State one benefit of fasting for the ummah.

units.activity: Make a calendar page for the Islamic year with Ramadan, 'Id al-Fitr, Dhu al-Hijjah and 'Id al-Adha. Beside each write the meaning, three customs, one symbol and one social benefit. Then write a part (c) answer plan about whether Muslims should follow traditional or modern methods to determine the start of Ramadan.

check.q: What is iftar?
o: The meal to break the fast

check.q: What do Muslims remember on 'Id al-Adha?
Which night is believed to be better than a thousand months?

units.title: Islam (I5 and I6): Rites of Passage, Family, Shari'ah and Social Action
units.summary: Define, describe and explain birth rites, marriage, funerals, halal and haram, family teaching, the ummah, Shari'ah and its sources, zakah and sadaqah, khalifahs of the environment and Muslim charities.

sections.h: I5.1 Birth rites
p: Teach what happens and why.
• Adhan and iqamah: the father or an elder whispers the adhan into the baby's right ear and the iqamah into the left, so that the first words the baby hears are about God.
• Tahnik: rubbing something sweet, such as a chewed date, on the baby's gums, a custom of the Prophet.
• Tasmiyah: the naming. A good name is chosen, often on the seventh day.
• Head shaving and sadaqah: the baby's head is shaved and charity equal to the weight of the hair in silver or gold is given.
• Aqiqah: a sacrifice of an animal (usually one or two) with the meat shared with family and the poor. It celebrates the birth and thanks God.
• Circumcision for boys: a practice of the Prophet Ibrahim and of Muslims.
• Importance: welcoming the child into the faith community and thanking God.

b: Hearing the adhan links the baby to tawhid.
Charity shows that new life is a blessing to be shared.
Different communities do these customs in different ways and times.

sections.h: I5.2 and I5.3 Marriage and funerals
p: Marriage:
• Nikah: the Muslim marriage ceremony and legal contract (aqd nikah). Both bride and groom must agree freely. The imam usually leads it.
• Mahr: a gift (dowry) from the groom to the bride, which belongs to her.
• Witnesses: usually two witnesses attend the signing of the contract.
• Walimah: the wedding feast, which the groom hosts, often after the nikah.
• Customs before, during and after: henna, music, special clothes and prayers differ by culture.
Funerals:
• Views: the purpose of life is to worship God. Muslims believe in the sovereignty of God and akhirah, so death is a transition.

• Rituals: the shahadah is said to the dying; after death the body is washed (ghusl), wrapped in plain white cloth (kafan), funeral prayer (janazah) is said, and burial takes place as soon as possible, with the body facing Makkah.

• Mourning: for three days in general, and widows observe a longer waiting period ('iddah) of four months and ten days. Differences exist in how long families mourn and how it is shown. Reasons include culture and interpretation.

b: Some Muslim cultures hold large wedding celebrations; others very simple ones.
Mourning practices differ: some hold gatherings on the third and fortieth day; others do not.
Teachers: describe each as a custom, not as the only 'true' way.

sections.h: I5.4 and I5.5 Family life, halal and haram, tradition and change
p: The family is the basic unit of the community in Islam.

• Halal and haram: halal means permitted and haram means forbidden. For food: halal includes meat from animals slaughtered in the name of God, and haram includes pork, blood and alcohol. For clothing: modest dress; the style differs among Muslim communities.

• Roles and responsibilities of men and women: traditional teaching says men provide and protect; women care for the home and children, but women can also work and own property. Views on how this is applied vary.
• Nurture of the young and care of the elderly: parents must educate children; children must honour and care for their parents (the Qur'an, Surah 17).
• Marriage, divorce and remarriage: marriage is encouraged and divorce is allowed but discouraged. Talaq is a husband's divorce; khul' is a woman's right to initiate divorce.

• Tradition and change: some communities keep traditional roles; others support changes such as women's education and work. Social change can create emotional and spiritual challenges, for example between generations.

b: 'Traditional family roles are best for Muslim families.' Evaluate.
For: stable, follows long tradition, clear responsibilities.
Against: modern needs, women's education and work, equal partnership.
Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.

sections.h: I6.1 and I6.2 The ummah and Shari'ah
p: Define and explain the key terms.
• Ummah: the worldwide Muslim community. It gives a sense of belonging, shared responsibility and support.
• Shari'ah ('straight path'): the code of behaviour and ethics for Muslims, and a legal system. It covers worship, family life, business and conduct.
• Sources of Shari'ah: the Qur'an and the sunnah (the example and sayings of the Prophet, found in hadith).
• Fiqh ('understanding'): the study of Islamic law to understand God's law.
• Ijtihad: independent reasoning or 'intellectual struggle' by qualified scholars to give judgements on new issues.
• Ijma': agreement among qualified scholars.
• Qiyas: reasoning by analogy, comparing a new case with a similar one in the Qur'an or sunnah.
• Halal and haram: thoughts and actions that are permitted or forbidden, drawn from Shari'ah.

b: The Qur'an forbids wine (an intoxicant).
Scholars reason that other intoxicating drugs are forbidden for the same reason.
This is qiyas: using a similar reason for a new case.

sections.h: I6.3 and I6.4 Concern for others and khalifahs of the environment
p: Muslim teaching about love, compassion and concern for others.

• Zakah: obligatory charity, one of the Five Pillars. It is usually 2.5% of savings above a set amount (nisab) each year, given to the poor, those in debt and other groups named in the Qur'an. It purifies wealth.
• Sadaqah: voluntary giving of money, time, kind words or help at any time.
• What they can and cannot be used for: they can help people in need, feed the hungry, pay for education and health; they cannot be used to pay for a wealthy person's expenses or for wrongdoing.
• Wealth is loaned by God: Muslims believe wealth belongs to God and that they will be judged on how they treated others.
Khalifahs of the environment:
• Humans are khalifahs (stewards) of the Earth for God.
• God created everything and humans must care for the Earth. This can include saving water, planting trees and avoiding waste.
• The syllabus note: the focus is Muslim stewardship of the environment, not debates on treatment of animals.

b: Zakah: compulsory, fixed amount, yearly.
Sadaqah: voluntary, any amount, any time.
Both: help the poor and purify the giver's heart.

sections.h: I6.5 Muslim organisations that relieve poverty
p: Teach what each organisation does and why Muslims support it.
• Muslim Aid: an international charity that responds to poverty, disasters and education needs, motivated by Islamic teaching.
• The Red Crescent: the sister organisation of the Red Cross in many Muslim-majority countries, giving emergency relief and healthcare.
• Groups and organisations specific to a country: local charities, mosque funds, zakat committees and relief groups. Teach at least one from your students' context.
• Concern for spiritual and physical needs: many Muslim groups provide food and shelter and also education and religious guidance.
• Motivation: Qur'an teachings on charity, justice and mercy, and the example of the Prophet, who cared for the poor and orphans.

b: 'Zakah is the best way to end poverty.' Evaluate.
For: compulsory, regular, spreads wealth, supports many.
Against: needs good management; other causes of poverty need other solutions such as education and government policy.
Judgement: reasoned.

sections.h: Revision and common mistakes
p: Common mistakes.
• Mixing zakah (obligatory) and sadaqah (voluntary).
• Saying all Muslims share the same wedding or mourning customs.
• Confusing fiqh (understanding), ijtihad (independent judgement), ijma' (consensus) and qiyas (analogy).
• Saying halal only refers to food. It also includes behaviour and clothing.
Revision tasks:
• Make a four-box chart of fiqh, ijtihad, ijma' and qiyas with one example each.
• List birth, marriage and funeral rituals with their meaning.
• Write one part (b) explanation about zakah.

b: I can explain three birth rites and why they matter.
I can describe a nikah and a funeral.
I can define the four tools of fiqh.
I can name two Muslim charities and what they do.

units.activity: Create a 'Muslim Life Journey' timeline: birth (adhan, aqiqah), marriage (nikah, mahr, walimah), death (ghusl, janazah, burial), with one meaning for each. Add a box on zakah and sadaqah, and write a part (c) plan on whether charity is the most important duty of a Muslim.

check.q: What is mahr?
o: A gift from the groom to the bride

check.q: What is khul'?
o: A woman's right to initiate divorce

check.q: What does ijtihad mean?
o: Independent judgement or intellectual struggle by qualified scholars

units.title: Judaism (J1): Worship in the Synagogue, Shabbat, Ritual Dress and Leaders
units.summary: Define, describe and explain the synagogue and its features, worship objects, ritual dress, public and private prayer, the Torah, Shabbat and the roles of the rabbi and chazan.

sections.h: J1.1 The synagogue: centre for worship and for the community
p: In Judaism the syllabus writes God as G-d. Use this spelling when you teach and expect students to use it or a clear alternative.
• Synagogue: from the Greek for 'to bring together' or 'house of assembly'. It is a centre for Jewish worship.
• It is also the centre of the Jewish community: for prayer, study, celebrations, classes, social events and support.
• Other names: shul (Yiddish), temple (in some Reform communities).
• Jews can pray anywhere, but some prayers need a minyan (see J1.5), so the synagogue brings people together.

b: 'Explain why the synagogue is important to Jews.' It is where the community prays, studies the Torah and meets.
Link to evaluation: 'The home is more important than the synagogue for Jewish life.' Give views and a judgement.

sections.h: J1.2 Key features of a synagogue: define, describe and explain
p: Features differ among Jewish traditions. Teach each feature and its meaning.
• Aron ha-kodesh (Holy Ark): the cupboard or alcove that holds the Torah scrolls. It faces Jerusalem and is the holiest place. A curtain (parochet) often covers it.
• Sefer Torah (Torah scrolls): handwritten scrolls of the first five books of the Bible. They are the most sacred objects.
• Bimah: the raised reading desk or platform from which the Torah is read.
• Ner tamid (eternal light): a lamp that never goes out above the Ark. It reminds Jews of G-d's constant presence and of the lamp in the Temple.
• Ten Commandments: two tablets of the Law, often displayed above the Ark.
• Menorah: the seven-branched candlestick, a symbol of the Temple and of Judaism.
• Magen David: the Star or Shield of David, a six-pointed star, a symbol of Jewish identity.
• Absence of images: no statues or pictures of G-d or humans, because G-d cannot be represented and worship of images is forbidden (Second Commandment).
• Seating arrangements: Orthodox synagogues usually have men and women seated separately (often with a screen or balcony). Reform and Liberal synagogues usually have mixed seating.

b: Orthodox: separate seating, men lead the service.
Reform and Liberal: mixed seating, women may be rabbis and read from the Torah.
All: face Jerusalem and honour the Torah.

sections.h: J1.3 Artefacts and J1.4 ritual dress
p: Artefacts used in worship:
• Sefer Torah copies: read in services and carried with care.
• Shabbat candles: lit before sunset on Friday to welcome Shabbat.
• Challah: plaited bread, eaten on Shabbat and festivals. Two loaves recall the double portion of manna.
• Kiddush cup: a cup of wine used for the blessing (Kiddush) that makes Shabbat holy.
• Mikveh: a ritual bath for spiritual cleansing, used for conversion, before marriage and in some communities regularly.
• Mezuzah: a small case on the doorframe containing a scroll with the Shema ('Hear, Israel, the Lord our G-d, the Lord is one') and other verses. It reminds Jews of G-d's commandments.
Ritual dress:
• Tallit: a prayer shawl with 613 tassels (tzitzit), to remember all the commandments.
• Tefillin: small leather boxes with Torah verses, worn on the arm and head at weekday morning prayer.
• Kippah or yarmulke: a skull cap showing respect for G-d.
• Views: in Orthodox practice, men wear them; in Reform and Liberal communities, women may also wear them.

b: Tefillin: bind the commandments to the mind and heart.
Tzitzit: 613 knots and threads remind the wearer of the commandments.
Kippah: a reminder that G-d is above.

sections.h: J1.5 Public and private worship and Torah study
p: Teach the main forms and views.
• Minyan: the minimum number of people for some public prayers, ten adult Jews. In Orthodox communities, ten men; in Reform and Liberal communities, ten adults including women.
• Communal prayer in the synagogue and the home: prayer is said three times daily (morning, afternoon and evening) by many Jews. Shabbat and festival services are communal.
• Daily private prayer: said in the synagogue or the home. A devotional practice that keeps G-d in daily life.
• Different views: Orthodox Jews place great weight on regular communal prayer; some Reform and Liberal Jews pray less often but still value it.
• Study of the Torah: in the synagogue and at home. Study is seen as an act of worship.
• Use of the Torah: read aloud in services; kept in the Ark; studied privately.

• Respectful treatment of the Torah scrolls: Torah scrolls are never touched by hand (a yad or pointer is used), are kept in a decorated cover, carried with care and never dropped or put on the floor.

b: 'Public worship is more important than private prayer for Jews.' Evaluate.
For: minyan, community, shared tradition, certain prayers need ten.
Against: personal relationship with G-d, home rituals, private study.
Judgement: reasoned.

sections.h: J1.6 Shabbat: synagogue and home
p: Shabbat (the Sabbath) is the weekly day of rest from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall. It remembers creation and rest, and the exodus from Egypt.
• Friday evening meal: preparation and cleaning, lighting Shabbat candles to welcome Shabbat, Kiddush over wine, the blessing over challah, a family meal with songs and prayers.
• Synagogue services: Friday evening and Saturday morning services, including the Kiddush and other blessings, the reading from the Sefer Torah of the weekly portion (Sidrah), prayers and a sermon.
• Observance: no work, no driving or use of electricity in many Orthodox homes; others interpret the rules differently.
• Havdalah ('division'): the ceremony that ends Shabbat, with wine, spices and a plaited candle, in the synagogue and at home. It separates the holy day from the rest of the week.
• Meaning and importance: rest, family, community and a weekly reminder of G-d.

b: Orthodox: strict rules about work and travel.
Reform and Liberal: more freedom, with the emphasis on family and rest.
All: Shabbat is a joyful day.

sections.h: J1.7 Leaders in the synagogue
p: Jewish leaders guide the community in study and worship.

• Rabbi: a Jewish scholar or teacher. Rabbis teach, give sermons, advise on Jewish law, lead services and weddings and funerals, and support the community. In Reform and Liberal communities, women can be rabbis; in Orthodox communities, only men.
• Chazan (cantor): leads the people in singing the prayers in worship. The chazan has a trained voice and knows the melodies.
• Lay leaders: community members who help run services, read from the Torah and support the synagogue.
• Different views: in some communities the rabbi is a leader with authority; in others the congregation shares more of the decisions.

b: Explain the role of the rabbi.
Teaching, leading worship, giving advice, officiating at life events.
Link: this shows the synagogue as a community centre.

sections.h: Revision and common mistakes
p: Common mistakes.
• Mixing up the Ark (the cupboard) and the bimah (the reading desk).
• Saying all Jews pray in the same way.
• Writing 'God' without noting the syllabus spelling G-d.
• Treating the tallit and the kippah as the same object.
