• Forgetting that the Torah has special respect rules.
Revision tasks:
• Label a synagogue plan with Ark, bimah, ner tamid and seating.
• Make a two-column table: Orthodox and Reform views on seating, minyan, dress and women's roles.
• Write a six-mark explanation of Shabbat.

b: I can name and explain nine synagogue features.
I can explain Shabbat from Friday evening to Havdalah.
I can give two views on women's roles in worship.
I can write a part (c) question on public and private prayer.

units.activity: Draw a labelled synagogue plan showing the Aron ha-kodesh, bimah, ner tamid, menorah and seating. Write a one-line meaning for each feature. Add a timeline of Shabbat from Friday candles to Havdalah. Then write a part (b) answer on 'Explain the importance of Shabbat for Jews'.

check.q: What is the aron ha-kodesh?
o: The Holy Ark that holds the Torah scrolls

check.q: What is the minimum number needed for public prayer called?
What does Havdalah mark?

units.title: Judaism (J2 and J3): Beliefs, Covenants, Torah, Pilgrimage and Memory
units.summary: Define, describe and explain Jewish beliefs about G-d, the covenants with Abraham and Moses, the Torah and mitzvot, pilgrimage, the Western Wall, Yad Vashem and the memory of the Temple.

sections.h: J2.1 Jewish beliefs about G-d's nature
p: Teach each belief with a short explanation and an example.
• G-d is one: the heart of Jewish belief, said in the Shema ('Hear, O Israel, the Lord our G-d, the Lord is one').
• G-d is merciful and just: G-d forgives and also holds people to account.
• G-d is the creator and sustainer of all things: G-d made the universe and keeps it going.
• G-d has no body: Jews do not picture G-d in human form.
• G-d is omnipotent (all powerful), omniscient (all knowing) and omnipresent (everywhere).
• Different views: Jews hold a range of views about how to understand these ideas; some stress tradition, others reinterpret in modern terms.
• Impact on daily life: Jews pray, keep commandments, and try to act justly and with compassion.

b: 'State what Jews believe about G-d's nature.' One, creator, just and merciful.
'Explain why belief in one G-d matters.' It shapes worship; there is no idol worship; it unites all Jews.

sections.h: J2.2 G-d's covenants with the Jewish people
p: A covenant is an agreement. The syllabus names two.
• Covenant with Abraham: G-d promised Abraham land and many descendants. The sign of the covenant is circumcision. In return Abraham and his descendants must believe in the one G-d.
• Covenant with Moses at Mount Sinai: G-d gave the commandments (the Ten Commandments and the 613 mitzvot). G-d promised protection if the people obeyed. Moses recorded the covenant.

• Importance: the covenants set up the relationship between G-d and the Jewish people. Jews are called 'the chosen people', which many understand as chosen for responsibility, not superiority. The covenant shows a complete way of life.
• Different views: some see the covenant as binding for all Jewish law; others see it as a source of values.
• Impact on daily life: observing mitzvot, keeping circumcision (brit milah), study and prayer.

b: Abraham: land, descendants, circumcision, faith in one G-d.
Moses: law, protection, 613 commandments, written record.
Both: shape Jewish identity.

sections.h: J2.3 Jewish beliefs about the Torah
p: The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy). It is also a general word for Jewish teaching.
• As a source of authority: Jews follow its commandments (mitzvot).
• As a revelation from G-d: believed to be given to Moses at Sinai. Orthodox Jews hold that every word comes from G-d; Reform and Liberal Jews see it as inspired and written by people.

• As a source of moral principles: positive mitzvot (things Jews should do, such as honour parents and give to the poor) and negative mitzvot (things Jews should not do, such as steal or murder). The Ten Commandments are a central summary.
• Noahide laws: seven laws for all humanity, including not to murder, steal, worship idols or commit certain sins, and to set up courts of justice.
• Importance in Jewish life: the Torah guides worship, family life, food, work and justice.

b: Orthodox: the mitzvot are binding and unchanging.
Conservative: the tradition can develop.
Reform: individuals decide which mitzvot to keep, guided by ethics.

sections.h: J3.1 Pilgrimage for some Jews
p: Pilgrimage is not compulsory for modern Jews, but many find it meaningful. In ancient times Jews went to the Temple in Jerusalem for the three pilgrim festivals: Pesach, Shavuot and Sukkot.
• Spiritual goals: to pray in a holy place, to feel connected to Jewish history and to remember the Temple.
• Physical goals: to travel to Israel and visit historic sites.
• Challenges: cost, travel, security concerns and emotional intensity.
• Effects: a deeper sense of identity and belonging, and for some a sense of 'coming home'.

b: Some Jews go on pilgrimage to deepen their connection to Jewish history.
Some choose to go for important life events such as Bar Mitzvah.
Others feel that daily prayer and study are more important than travel.

sections.h: J3.2 The historic sites of Jerusalem
p: Teach what each place is, what happens there and why it is important.
• The Western Wall (also called the Kotel):
• It is the last remaining fragment of the wall that surrounded the Second Temple, which the Romans destroyed in 70 CE.
• It is important for some Jews to visit the site of the Temple, the holiest place in Judaism.
• Practices: praying, placing notes with prayers in the cracks, touching the wall, and holding Bar and Bat Mitzvah celebrations. Men and women pray in separate areas in the traditional arrangement.
• Yad Vashem (Holocaust Memorial):
• It is a memorial to the Holocaust and a place of information and education.
• Some Jews use the term 'Shoah' (catastrophe) for the Holocaust, and remembering the events is important to Jews today to honour the victims, teach future generations and prevent it happening again.

• Sites of great significance: the cattle car, the children's memorial, the Hall of Remembrance, the Hall of Names, Janusz Korczak Square and the Avenue of the Righteous Among the Nations (honouring non-Jews who saved Jews).

b: The Holocaust is a sensitive topic. Teach it with facts and respect.
Warn students beforehand and allow quiet reflection.
Focus on memory, learning and honouring the victims.

sections.h: J3.3 Keeping the memory of the Temple alive
p: After the Temple was destroyed, Judaism changed from Temple worship to synagogue worship, study and prayer. The memory of the Temple is kept alive in many ways.
• Visiting the Western Wall.
• The importance given to the Ark and the ner tamid in the synagogue, which echo the Ark of the Covenant and the lamp in the Temple.
• Daily prayers today follow the same pattern as worship in the Temple.
• Some prayers ask for the rebuilding of the Temple and a time of peace.
• Different views: Orthodox Jews hope for a rebuilt Temple. Many Reform Jews see the Temple as a memory of the past and focus on the synagogue as the centre of worship.

b: 'The Western Wall is the most important place in Judaism today.' Evaluate.
For: link to the Temple, prayer, history, community.
Against: the synagogue is the daily centre of worship; Jewish life continues everywhere.
Judgement: reasoned.

sections.h: Revision and common mistakes
p: Common mistakes.
• Saying the Western Wall is the Temple. It is a remaining part of the wall around the Temple.
• Confusing the covenants with Abraham and Moses.
• Saying all Jews understand the Torah in the same way.
• Using the word Holocaust without explaining Shoah and the importance of memory.
Revision tasks:
• Two-column table: Abraham covenant | Moses covenant.
• Three sentences about the Torah as authority, revelation and moral guide.
• One paragraph on why Yad Vashem matters.

b: I can state seven beliefs about G-d.
I can compare the two covenants.
I can explain the Western Wall and Yad Vashem.
I can give two views on the Temple.

units.activity: Create a one-page poster 'Jewish Beliefs and Sacred Places'. Include: five beliefs about G-d, the two covenants, three uses of the Torah, and a mini-map of Jerusalem with the Western Wall and Yad Vashem. Write a part (c) plan on whether pilgrimage is important for modern Jews.

check.q: Which covenant has circumcision as its sign?
What is the Western Wall?
o: The last remaining fragment of the wall around the Temple

check.q: What are Noahide laws?

units.title: Judaism (J4): Festivals and Fasts
units.summary: Define, describe and explain Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Pesach and Sukkot with their religious reasons, social significance and different ways of observing, and how practice changes today.

sections.h: A pattern for each festival
p: Use these questions for every festival.
• What is it, and when does it happen (Jewish calendar)?
• What does it remember?
• How is it kept in the synagogue and at home?
• Religious reasons: origins, purpose and symbolism.
• Social significance.
• Different ways it is observed.
• Changes and different feelings today.
Remember: the Jewish calendar is lunar with extra months added so festivals stay in the right season.

b: The syllabus removed Simchat Torah and Shavuot in 2025. Teach Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Pesach and Sukkot.

sections.h: J4.1 Rosh Hashanah (Jewish New Year)
p: Rosh Hashanah means 'Head of the Year'.
• It begins the Ten Days of Awe (Days of Repentance), a time for reflection and asking forgiveness, ending with Yom Kippur.
• It celebrates G-d's Creation.
• The Book of Life: Jews believe G-d judges people and writes their fate for the year. The greeting 'May you be inscribed in the Book of Life' reflects this.
• Shofar blowing in synagogue services: the ram's horn is blown as a wake-up call to repent and to remember G-d as king.
• Special foods: apples dipped in honey and sweet foods for a sweet new year, round challah for the cycle of the year.
• Tashlikh (casting away): going to flowing water and symbolically casting away sins by throwing in bread crumbs.
• Religious reasons: renewal, repentance and trust in G-d's mercy.
• Social significance: family meals, new year cards and greetings, visits.
• Different ways: Orthodox Jews keep two days; Reform Jews may keep one; customs vary between communities.

b: Shofar: wake-up call.
Apple and honey: a sweet year.
Round challah: the circle of the year.
Tashlikh: casting away sin.

sections.h: J4.2 Yom Kippur (Day of Atonement)
p: Yom Kippur is the holiest day of the Jewish year.
• It is the last of the Ten Days of Awe.

• Repentance is shown through fasting (about 25 hours, with no food or drink), prohibitions (no work, no washing for pleasure, no leather shoes, no perfume) and wearing white, which stands for purity.
• Reconciliation and new resolutions: before Yom Kippur Jews ask forgiveness of people they have wronged; they make a resolution to do better.

• Key features of the services: services last most of the day, with prayers of confession (Vidui), the Kol Nidre prayer on the evening before, readings and a final service (Ne'ilah) at the end, closing with a long shofar blast.
• Religious reasons: atonement, forgiveness and a fresh start with G-d.
• Social significance: the community comes together in synagogue; many who rarely attend come on this day.
• Different ways: some Jews fast fully; others, such as the ill, do not fast; Reform communities may keep fewer restrictions.

b: The sick, elderly, pregnant women and children are exempt from fasting.
Saving a life always comes before fasting.
Different communities apply rules differently.

sections.h: J4.3 Pesach (Passover)
p: Pesach is a spring festival lasting seven or eight days.
• It celebrates G-d's deliverance of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt, through the final plague (the death of the firstborn) and the Exodus. G-d 'passed over' the houses of the Israelites.
• The Seder (order) meal on the first night (and second night outside Israel): families gather to retell the story using the Haggadah, the book that sets out the order.

• The Seder plate: karpas (green vegetable dipped in salt water, for tears), maror (bitter herbs, for the bitterness of slavery), charoset (sweet paste, for the mortar), zeroa (shank bone, for the Pesach sacrifice) and beitzah (roasted egg, for new life and festival offerings).

• Other items: matzah (unleavened bread, because the Israelites left in haste), four cups of wine (for four promises of G-d), a cup for Elijah and the four questions, usually asked by the youngest child, starting 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
• Religious reasons: freedom and G-d's saving power.
• Social significance: families and guests, welcoming strangers.
• Different ways: Ashkenazi and Sephardi foods differ; some communities keep seven days and some eight; no leavened food (chametz) is eaten.

b: Karpas: spring and tears.
Maror: bitterness.
Charoset: mortar.
Zeroa: sacrifice.
Beitzah: new life.

sections.h: J4.4 Sukkot (Booths or Tabernacles)
p: Sukkot lasts seven days in autumn.
• It celebrates the gathering of the harvest and G-d's protection of the Israelites during their 40 years in the wilderness.
• Building and using a sukkah: a temporary hut with a roof of branches through which stars can be seen. Jews eat, and some sleep, in it. It reminds them of the wilderness and shows trust in G-d.

• The waving of the lulav and etrog: four species of plant: the lulav (palm), etrog (citron), hadass (myrtle) and aravah (willow). They are held together and waved in all directions during prayers to show G-d is everywhere.
• Religious reasons: thanksgiving, trust and remembering history.
• Social significance: building the sukkah together, inviting guests, family meals.
• Different ways: some families have large sukkot at home; others use the synagogue sukkah; weather and space affect customs.

b: Pesach: freedom from slavery; matzah and Seder.
Sukkot: protection in the wilderness; sukkah and lulav.
Both: remember the Exodus and G-d's care.

sections.h: J4.5 Changes to festivals and fasts
p: Teach how practice is changing and how Jews feel about it.
• Changes in the modern world: many Jews keep customs while living busy lives; online Seders, shorter services, family-friendly celebrations and diverse practice.
• Different views: Orthodox Jews usually want to keep traditional practice. Reform and Liberal Jews adapt practice to modern life.
• Feelings: some feel change keeps the faith alive and welcoming. Others fear loss of tradition and identity.

b: 'Jewish festivals should be kept in the traditional way.' Evaluate.
For: link to history, identity, obedience to G-d.
Against: needs of modern life, inclusion, diverse practice.
Judgement: reasoned.

sections.h: Revision table and common mistakes
p: Use this table:
• Rosh Hashanah | New Year, autumn | Creation and judgement | shofar, apple and honey.
• Yom Kippur | 10 Tishrei | atonement | fasting, white clothes.
• Pesach | spring | Exodus | Seder, matzah.
• Sukkot | autumn | harvest and wilderness | sukkah, lulav.
Common mistakes: confusing Rosh Hashanah with Yom Kippur; forgetting the symbolism of the Seder foods; saying every Jew fasts the same way; describing customs without meaning.

b: Name two Seder foods and their meaning.
Explain why the shofar is blown.
State one social significance of Sukkot.

units.activity: Create a 'Jewish Festival Year' chart with Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Pesach and Sukkot. For each write the meaning, three customs, one symbol and one social significance. Then write a part (c) plan on whether festivals should be kept in a traditional way.

check.q: What does the shofar do on Rosh Hashanah?
o: Calls people to repent and remember G-d as king

check.q: What does matzah represent?
What are the four species of Sukkot?

units.title: Judaism (J5 and J6): Rites of Passage, Kashrut, Family and Social Action
units.summary: Define, describe and explain Brit Milah, naming, Bar and Bat Mitzvah, marriage, funerals and mourning, kashrut, family teaching, tzedakah, tikkun olam and Jewish charities.

sections.h: J5.1 Birth rites
p: Teach the main rites and the meaning of each.

• Brit Milah (covenant of circumcision): performed on a baby boy on the eighth day, by a mohel (trained circumciser). The sandek is the person on whose knee the baby is placed, usually a grandfather or honoured relative. The baby is given his Hebrew name. Meaning: the baby enters the covenant with G-d made with Abraham.
• Rituals in the ceremony: blessings over wine, naming, and a celebration meal.

• Naming ceremonies: girls are given their names in a ceremony in the synagogue or at home, often called Simchat Bat or Zeved HaBat. Many communities hold them on the first Shabbat after birth or in the first month.
• Different views: Orthodox and Reform practice may differ in naming for girls; some Reform communities have a parallel ceremony of covenant for girls.

b: It continues Abraham's covenant.
It joins the child to the Jewish people.
It is a family and community celebration.

sections.h: J5.2 Coming of age: Bar and Bat Mitzvah and Bat Chayil
p: These mark the age at which a young Jew takes on responsibility for the commandments.
• Bar Mitzvah (son of the commandment): for boys, at age 13.
• Bat Mitzvah (daughter of the commandment): for girls, at 12 in Orthodox communities and 12 or 13 in others.
• Lessons before the ceremony: learning Hebrew, the prayers, the meaning of the Torah reading and Jewish law.
• Main elements of the synagogue service: reading from the Torah (or a part of it), giving a talk about its meaning, leading prayers and being called to the Torah. A celebration meal follows.
• Bat Chayil (daughter of valour): in some Orthodox communities, girls celebrate with a ceremony and a talk, but may not read from the Torah.
• Importance: becoming a responsible adult in the community, able to take part in a minyan (in some communities).

b: Orthodox: Bat Mitzvah or Bat Chayil with no Torah reading in the main service.
Reform and Liberal: Bat Mitzvah with the same Torah reading as boys.
Both: celebrate responsibility and belonging.

sections.h: J5.3 and J5.4 Marriage and funeral rites
p: Marriage:
• Kiddushin (betrothal): the first stage, when the couple make their commitment. A ring is given and a blessing is said.

• The marriage ceremony takes place under the chuppah (canopy), a symbol of the new home. The ketubah (marriage contract) sets out the husband's duties to his wife and is signed by witnesses and read aloud. Seven blessings are said. The groom smashes a glass to remember the destruction of the Temple and that joy is mixed with sorrow.
Funeral rites:
• Preparation of the body: members of the Chevra Kaddisha (sacred society) wash the body and dress it in a simple white shroud; the person is not left alone before burial.
• Burial: usually within 24 hours, in a plain coffin or none in Israel. Kaddish, a prayer praising G-d, is recited.
• Candle: a candle is lit as a sign of the soul.

• Mourning rituals: the three stages are shiva (the first seven days, when mourners stay at home, sit on low stools and are visited), shloshim (30 days) and the year of mourning, with Kaddish said daily. The anniversary (yahrzeit) is marked with a candle and Kaddish.

ex.t: Why the glass is smashed (common explanations)
b: To remember the destruction of the Temple.
To remind the couple that life contains both joy and sorrow.
Guests shout 'Mazal tov' (good luck).

sections.h: J5.5 Kashrut (kosher and treyfah)
p: Kashrut is the set of laws about food that is 'fit' (kosher). Treyfah means 'forbidden'.
• Source: the Torah, especially Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14.

• Application to food: eat only animals that chew the cud and have cloven hooves (for example cows and sheep); fish with fins and scales; no pork, shellfish or birds of prey. Meat and dairy are kept apart, with separate dishes, pots and often separate kitchen areas. Animals must be killed in the ritual way (shechitah) and food prepared according to the rules. Food may be labelled with a kosher mark.
• Application to clothing and ritual objects: wool and linen are not mixed in clothing (shatnez), and objects such as tefillin and Torah scrolls must be made from kosher animals.

• Different views: Orthodox Jews follow the rules strictly. Reform and Liberal Jews may see them as personal choices or as ethical guidance. Some have reinterpreted the rules in modern ways. Reasons include obedience to G-d, discipline, holiness and community identity.
• Significance and relevance: some Jews see kashrut as central to Jewish life; others as less relevant.

b: 'Kashrut is no longer relevant for Jews today.' Evaluate.
For: modern life, difficulty of keeping, choice.
Against: identity, obedience to the Torah, community, discipline.
Judgement: reasoned.

sections.h: J5.6 and J5.7 The family; tradition and change
p: Family life is central to Jewish teaching.

• Roles and responsibilities: traditional roles gave women responsibility for the home and men for public religious duties, but there is strong respect for both. Many communities now emphasise equal partnership.
• Nurture and care of the elderly: parents teach children Torah and Jewish values; children honour and look after their parents (Fifth Commandment).

• Marriage, divorce and remarriage: marriage is highly valued. Divorce is allowed and a Jewish divorce is called a get; remarriage is possible. Orthodox communities follow strict rules about a get; Reform communities have different procedures.

• Tradition and change: some communities keep traditional roles and customs; others support change, such as women rabbis and changes in family structures. Social change can create emotional and spiritual challenges between generations.

b: Orthodox: keep traditional roles and rules about a get.
Reform: equal roles; individual choice in practice.
Teachers should present each fairly.

sections.h: J6 Religion and social action
p: Concern for others:
• Following the Torah's teaching on kindness: for example 'Love your neighbour as yourself' (Leviticus 19:18) and care for the poor, the stranger, widows and orphans.
• Tzedakah (righteous giving): giving to those in need is a duty; many Jews give about a tenth of income. It means justice more than charity.
• Pushkes: small collection boxes kept at home, in synagogues and schools for charity.
• Gemilut hasadim (kind actions): acts of kindness such as visiting the sick, comforting mourners and hosting guests.
Stewardship of the environment:
• Humans are stewards of the Earth for G-d.
• G-d created everything and people must care for it.
• Tikkun olam ('repair the world'): the idea that Jews should work to improve the world, including caring for the environment. The syllabus focus is environmental stewardship, not animal ethics.
Organisations that relieve poverty:
• Tzedek, Jewish Care and World Jewish Relief, and local groups.
• Their work: relieving poverty, caring for the elderly, disaster relief. Both spiritual and physical needs matter.
• Motivation: Jewish teachings on justice and kindness.

b: 'Tzedakah is the most important Jewish duty.' Evaluate.
For: helps the poor, commanded in the Torah, daily practice.
Against: other mitzvot such as prayer and Shabbat are also central.
Judgement: reasoned.

sections.h: Revision checklist and common mistakes
p: Common mistakes.
• Saying all Jewish families keep kosher in the same way.
• Mixing Bar and Bat Mitzvah customs across communities.
• Forgetting the three stages of mourning.
• Confusing tzedakah with ordinary charity.
Checklist:
• I can describe brit milah and two naming customs.
• I can explain Bar and Bat Mitzvah with two views.
• I can describe a Jewish wedding and funeral.
• I can explain kashrut with examples and different views.
• I can define tzedakah, gemilut hasadim and tikkun olam.

b: Explain one reason for kashrut.
Name the three stages of mourning.
Give one example of tikkun olam.

units.activity: Create a 'Jewish Life Journey' chart: birth, coming of age, marriage, death. For each, write what happens, the meaning and one different view. Add a box on kashrut with five rules and one reason. Then write a part (c) plan on whether kashrut is still relevant.

check.q: What is a ketubah?
What is shiva?
o: The first seven days of mourning

check.q: What does tikkun olam mean?

units.title: Details of the Assessment: Paper 1, Paper 2 and the Structure of Questions
units.summary: Understand exactly what each paper tests, how many questions students answer, how parts (a), (b) and (c) work, the timing and the advice for evaluation answers.

sections.h: Paper 1: Worship, Beliefs, Scriptures and Sacred Places
p: Paper 1 is a written paper.
• Time and marks: 1 hour 45 minutes, 80 marks, 50% of the grade.
• Content tested: topics 1, 2 and 3 for each religion (Worship; Beliefs and scriptures; Sacred places).
• Christianity topics C1, C2, C3. Islam topics I1, I2, I3. Judaism topics J1, J2, J3.
• Sections: A Christianity, B Islam, C Judaism.
• Choice: candidates choose two of the three sections (the two religions they have studied). In each chosen section they answer two of three structured questions.
• Total: four questions, each worth 20 marks.
• Externally assessed (marked by Cambridge).

ex.t: Example: a candidate who studied Christianity and Judaism
b: Chooses Section A and Section C.
Answers two of three questions in Section A.
Answers two of three questions in Section C.
Total: four 20-mark questions = 80 marks.

sections.h: Paper 2: Festivals, Fasts, Family Life and Social Action
p: Paper 2 has the same format as Paper 1.
• Time and marks: 1 hour 45 minutes, 80 marks, 50% of the grade.
• Content tested: topics 4, 5 and 6 (Festivals and fasts; Rites of passage and religion and the family; Religion and social action).
• Christianity topics C4, C5, C6. Islam topics I4, I5, I6. Judaism topics J4, J5, J6.
• Sections A, B and C again. Candidates answer two of the three structured questions in each of their two chosen sections.
• Candidates should use the same two religions in both papers.
• Externally assessed.

b: Paper 1: places, people, beliefs and scriptures.
Paper 2: calendar, life events, family and action in society.
Both papers: same time, same marks, same structure, same AO weighting.

sections.h: Structure of every question: parts (a), (b) and (c)
p: Every question is worth 20 marks. Candidates answer all parts of the chosen question.
• Part (a): 6 marks. A short-answer question assessing AO1 Knowledge and understanding. It has two sub-parts, (i) and (ii). It usually asks for facts. One mark is awarded for each relevant point.
• Part (b): 6 marks. Assesses AO1. It usually needs a more detailed description and/or explanation. It is marked with the levels-of-response marking grid for AO1.

• Part (c): 8 marks. Assesses AO2 Evaluation, linked to the same overall topic. It needs a longer structured response that evaluates different points of view and gives a judgement. It is marked with the levels-of-response grid for AO2.
• Teachers should encourage students to look at the marks available when answering: a 2-mark part needs two points, not a paragraph.
• The balance is 12 marks of AO1 and 8 marks of AO2 in each question, so AO1 is 60% and AO2 is 40%.

ex.t: Time guide (a suggestion, not an official rule)
b: 105 minutes for four questions is about 26 minutes per question.
Part (a): about 5 minutes. Part (b): about 8 minutes. Part (c): about 12 minutes.
Leave 3 to 5 minutes at the end to check.

sections.h: Advice for part (c) Evaluation answers
p: The syllabus gives clear advice about part (c). Teach it step by step.
• The question presents an issue where different points of view can be held.
• More than one point of view can be two opposing views (agree and disagree), but any views that differ from each other are enough.
• Answers must be in well-structured continuous prose, with paragraphs.
• Each paragraph states and then considers a point of view or argument.
• A point of view must be supported with evidence (a belief, teaching, practice or example).
• Answers should not be descriptive. They should focus on the specific question, not on broad themes linked to it.
• A firm, clear judgement: the examiner should see the position taken. The judgement should be reasoned and should build on the evidence before it.
• Candidates may draw on material from across the syllabus for that paper to present a range of arguments.
• Candidates are not penalised for using a different spelling to the syllabus, as long as it is clear which word they mean.

b: Point: state one view in a sentence.
Evidence: a teaching, belief or practice that supports it.
Explain: link the evidence to the question.
Link or counter: bring in a different view.
Judgement: end with a reasoned conclusion that answers the question.

sections.h: Marking: levels of response and specimen mark schemes
p: Parts (b) and (c) are marked with levels-of-response marking grids. The grids are published in the specimen mark schemes at www.cambridgeinternational.org/0490 and on the School Support Hub. Download them and read them before you start marking.
How levels of response work in general (the exact grid is in the specimen mark scheme):
• Examiners read the whole answer and decide which level describes it best.
• Then they choose a mark within the level, depending on how well the answer fits.
• Part (a) is marked point by point: one mark for each relevant point.
• For AO1, higher levels show accurate, detailed, well-developed knowledge and understanding with examples and links between ideas.
• For AO2, higher levels show clear arguments for different views, supported by evidence, with a well-reasoned judgement.
Important: Grade descriptions for this syllabus are not yet published. Use the specimen mark schemes.

• Plan part (c) in three lines before writing: two views and a judgement.
• Write in paragraphs for (b) and (c). Bullet points may be used in part (a) if each point is clear.
• Use the vocabulary of the religion correctly and explain it.

units.title: Command Words and Exam Technique: Worked Examples for Parts (a), (b) and (c)
units.summary: Learn the 11 command words with examples, and see model answers and marking notes for each part of a question, written for training and not taken from a Cambridge paper.

sections.h: What command words are and why they matter
p: Command words are the key verbs in a question. They tell the candidate what to do. If a student misreads the command word, the answer often earns few marks even when the knowledge is right.
• The syllabus lists 11 command words and gives each a meaning.
• The way a word is used depends on the subject context.
• Part (a) usually uses simple words (identify, state, give, outline).
• Part (b) usually uses describe or explain.
• Part (c) uses evaluation words, such as evaluate, assess, discuss, comment and compare.
Teach the words early and keep a poster on the wall.

b: Students circle the command word before writing.
Then write it in the margin with its meaning.
This takes five seconds and prevents the most common error.

sections.h: The 11 command words: meaning and example
p: Use these meanings from the syllabus. The examples are written for this course, not taken from a Cambridge paper.
• Assess: make an informed judgement. Example: 'Assess the importance of the Five Pillars for Muslims.'
• Comment: give an informed opinion. Example: 'Comment on the view that pilgrimage is a hard journey.'
• Compare: identify and comment on similarities and/or differences. Example: 'Compare the ways Christians celebrate Christmas and Easter.'
• Describe: state the points of a topic and give characteristics and main features. Example: 'Describe a synagogue service on Shabbat.'
• Discuss: write about issues or topics in depth in a structured way. Example: 'Discuss the role of the Pope.'
• Evaluate: judge or calculate the quality, importance, amount or value of something. Example: 'Evaluate the statement that fasting is the most important part of Ramadan.'
• Explain: set out purposes or reasons; make relationships between things clear; say why and/or how and support with relevant evidence. Example: 'Explain why Jews use a mezuzah.'
• Give: produce an answer from a given source or from recall or memory. Example: 'Give two names of Muslim charities.'
• Identify: name, select or recognise. Example: 'Identify two features of a mosque.'
• Outline: set out the main points. Example: 'Outline how Christians prepare for Easter.'
• State: express in clear terms. Example: 'State what Muslims mean by tawhid.'

b: Short recall: identify, state, give, outline.
Detail: describe, explain.
Judgement: assess, comment, compare, discuss, evaluate.

sections.h: Worked example: part (a) (6 marks, one mark for each relevant point)
p: Training question set (about Christianity, C1, written for this course, not a Cambridge question).
• Part (a) has two sub-parts, (i) and (ii), worth 6 marks in total. For training we use two sub-parts of 3 marks each.
• Training (a)(i): State three features of a church building. (3 marks) Model answer: altar, pulpit, font. (1 mark each)

• Training (a)(ii): Outline three things that happen at the Eucharist. (3 marks) Model answer: readings are said, prayers are offered, bread and wine are shared in memory of the Last Supper. (1 mark each)
Marking notes:
• One mark for each relevant point. Do not give extra marks for repeated points.
• A correct word without explanation can earn the mark if it answers the question.
• Students should stop when they have given the number of points the marks suggest.

b: Writing a long paragraph for a 2-mark sub-part.
Giving the same point twice in different words.
Not reading 'two' or 'three' in the question.

sections.h: Worked example: part (b) (6 marks, levels of response)
p: Training question: 'Explain why the Eucharist is important to Christians.' (6 marks)
Model answer (written for training):

'The Eucharist is important to Christians because it remembers the Last Supper, when Jesus shared bread and wine with his disciples and told them to do this in memory of him. By sharing bread and wine, Christians remember Jesus' death and sacrifice for them. For Catholics and Orthodox Christians the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ, so it is a very holy moment when they receive Christ. For many Protestants it is a way to remember Jesus and show unity with other believers. It is also important because the Eucharist brings the church community together every week, and reminds them of forgiveness and new life.'
Why this answer works:
• It gives several reasons, each explained (remembering the Last Supper, sacrifice, holy presence, community).
• It uses correct religious language.
• It includes different Christian views.
• It stays on the question.

b: Weak: 'It is important because Christians do it every Sunday.' (one point, no explanation)
Better: add why it is done (Jesus told them), what it means (sacrifice), and who believes what (Catholic and Protestant).

sections.h: Worked example: part (c) (8 marks, AO2 Evaluation)
p: Training question: ''The Bible is the most important part of Christian worship.' Evaluate this statement.' (8 marks)
Model answer (written for training):

'Some Christians would agree. Many Protestants believe the Bible is the word of God, so hearing it read and explained in the sermon is the heart of worship. For example, in many Baptist churches the sermon is the longest part of the service, because they believe God speaks to people through scripture. On the other hand, Catholic and Orthodox Christians stress the Eucharist as the centre of worship. They believe it is the most direct way to meet Jesus, and the Bible readings lead to it. Other Christians, such as Quakers, would say that silent waiting for the Holy Spirit is equally or more important, because they believe God can speak to anyone directly. In my judgement, the Bible is very important in all Christian worship because it shapes prayers, hymns and sermons, but it is not the only important part. Most Christians combine scripture, prayer and sacrament, so I think it is the most important for some, but not for all Christians.'
Why this answer works:
• It gives different views and says who holds them.
• Each view has evidence.
• It stays focused on the question.
• It ends with a firm, reasoned judgement.

ex.t: Marking checklist for part (c) (a classroom tool)
b: Two or more different views, each in its own paragraph.
Evidence for each view (belief, teaching or practice).
No unneeded description.
A clear judgement that follows from the evidence.

p: Use these training questions (not official) to practise.

sections.h: Common mistakes and revision plan
p: Common mistakes across all parts.
• Not using the command word.
• Writing in bullet points for (c).
• Describing instead of evaluating.
• Giving only one view.
• Forgetting to name denominations or traditions.
• Giving personal beliefs.

• Week 3: part (b) explanations with peer marking.

• Week 5: timed full questions.
• Week 6: full timed papers and feedback.
